q-di-table.whatItIs: A grid of numbers (rows = years/cities/branches, columns = categories) with 5-6 questions hanging off it. Tests whether you can pull two numbers out of a grid without misreading the row, and run a percentage or ratio on them fast.
q-di-table.coreMethod:
1. Before touching any number: read the table title, the row header, the column header, and the UNITS line ('in thousands', 'in lakhs', 'figures in hundreds'). Circle the unit. A third of table-DI errors are unit errors, not arithmetic errors.
2. Scan all 5 question stems first — 15 seconds. Tag each on your rough sheet: D = direct two-number question, T = needs a row/column total, A = needs an average, X = needs everything. Note which totals are shared between questions.
3. Compute every SHARED total ONCE and write it in the margin beside the table. If Q2, Q4 and Q5 all need the 2023 column total, you compute it once and three questions collapse to one division each.
4. Attempt in the order D → T → A → X, never 1→5. The answer sheet does not know what order you used.
5. For each computation, look at the option spread before computing. If the two closest options differ by more than 5%, round every number to 2 significant figures and do it mentally.
6. For 'percent more/less' questions, write the fraction as (Bigger − Smaller) / BASE where BASE is the number that follows the word 'than'. Physically underline the word after 'than' in the stem before writing anything.
7. For ratio questions, cancel before multiplying: 4200:5600 → drop the 100s → 42:56 → divide by 14 → 3:4. Never long-divide a ratio.
8. Write each answer letter on the rough sheet next to its Q number as you go, then mark all 5 on screen in one pass. Saves 15-20 seconds of mouse travel per set.
tricks: Total reuse: in a 5×4 table, at most two totals are ever used across the 5 questions. Compute those two in the first 40 seconds and most of the set becomes single divisions.

Fraction recognition instead of division: if the options are 25%, 33.33%, 20%, 12.5%, 16.66%, these are 1/4, 1/3, 1/5, 1/8, 1/6. Check whether the difference is a clean fraction of the base — 350 more on a base of 1400 is 350/1400 = 1/4 = 25%. No long division at all.

Ratio comparison by cross-multiplication: for 'in which year was the ratio of A to B highest', do not compute five decimals. Compare a1/b1 vs a2/b2 by testing a1×b2 against a2×b1, keep the winner, run it against the next. Four comparisons, zero divisions.
Unit-digit elimination on 'find the total' questions: add only the unit digits of the column. With 4 or 5 numeric options, usually exactly one matches.

Percentage of a percentage in one step: if the table already gives percentages and the stem asks 'how many', multiply the percentage straight into the total using the 1/n fraction table rather than doing two separate multiplications.
If a 'Total' row or column is already printed on the table, never re-add it. Aspirants routinely spend 25 seconds re-summing a total that is sitting on the page.
traps: Unit mismatch between columns — one column in lakhs, another in thousands, or a footnote reading 'all figures in hundreds'. Every set contains exactly one question that only works if you noticed the unit line.
'A is what percent MORE than B' = (A−B)/B×100, but 'A is what percent OF B' = A/B×100. IBPS places both inside the same set, often consecutively, precisely to catch autopilot.
Row/column transposition — reading the 2022 row when the stem says the 2022 column. Keep your left index finger physically on the row label while your eye reads across.
'Except' and 'other than' wording: 'the total of all cities except Delhi' — the printed total INCLUDES Delhi. Subtract it.

Approximating a DIFFERENCE of two similar numbers. Rounding is safe for ratios and percentages, lethal for subtraction: 4980 − 4820 rounded becomes 5000 − 4800 = 200 instead of 160. Never round when subtracting two close values.
q-di-table.timeTarget: 3:30–4:00 min for a 5-question table set in Prelims (~45 sec/question); 4:30–5:00 in Mains where the grid is larger. The first 40 seconds go to reading plus shared totals, so questions 3, 4 and 5 must each land under 30 seconds.
q-di-table.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when, on a fresh 5×4 table set, you answer at least 4 of 5 correctly in under 3 minutes 30 seconds without writing a single long division — and when, asked immediately afterwards, you can recite the table's unit line from memory.

'The total of column P is approximately what percent of the total of column Q?'
'Find the average of [category] across all five years/branches.'
'In which year was the percentage increase over the previous year the highest?'
'The value of A in 2023 is what percent more/less than the value of B in 2021?'
'What is the difference between the total of row 1 and the total of row 4?'

q-di-bar.whatItIs: Vertical or horizontal bars, often two bars per category (double bar) or segmented (stacked). Adds exactly one skill over table DI: reading a value off a scale accurately and fast without re-reading it.
q-di-bar.coreMethod:
1. Read the y-axis scale first. Identify the gridline interval and write 'one line = ___' on your rough sheet before anything else.
2. Read the legend and say the mapping to yourself once ('dark = 2022, light = 2023'). Half of all double-bar errors are legend swaps, and they happen silently.
3. TRANSCRIBE every bar value into a small table on the rough sheet BEFORE answering anything. 30-40 seconds. This is the whole technique: you never re-read the graph, and you cannot misread the same bar twice.
4. If a bar lands between gridlines, the paper always intends a clean value. A bar between 60 and 80 is 70, never 68. If you get an ugly number, re-read the scale, not the bar.
5. Scan all 5 stems, mark which need totals, compute the shared totals once — same discipline as table DI.
6. For stacked bars, transcribe each segment AND the stack total. Stacked-bar questions are overwhelmingly 'segment as a percentage of the full bar'.
7. Attack direct comparisons first ('difference between A and B in year X'), leave five-term averages for last.
tricks: Transcribe-then-solve is the single biggest time saver in bar DI. Copy the 8-10 numbers in one pass, then work only from your sheet. It feels slower for 40 seconds and is faster by 60.

'Highest percentage increase' without computing four percentages: the biggest jump on the smallest base wins. Eyeball the pair where the gap is large relative to the SHORTER bar — usually only two candidates survive, so compute only those two.
In a double-bar set, 'in which year was the difference maximum' is answerable by eye. The largest visual gap IS the answer. Only compute if two gaps genuinely look equal.
Stacked bar: the unlabelled 'other/remaining' segment is total minus the printed segments. Compute it for every stack during transcription, not question by question.
For 'average of all bars', add by pairing values that make round numbers (340 + 260 = 600) rather than left to right.
If the chart is in percentages and the absolute total sits in a text line below, convert only the two bars you actually need — never convert all five.
traps: Legend swap in double-bar sets. At least one question per set is worded to punish reading the wrong series ('sales of company B in 2022' when B is the light bar and your eye went to the dark one).
A y-axis that does not start at zero, or major labels at 0/50/100/150 with minor gridlines every 10. Assuming every gridline is a major unit halves or doubles every answer in the set.
Combo charts carrying two different units — bars in thousands of units, an overlaid line in percent.
'Increase from 2021 to 2022' has base = 2021, the EARLIER year. Aspirants reflexively divide by the later, larger number.
Stacked bars where the stem asks about a segment but one option matches the whole bar — placed there for anyone who reads the top of the stack instead of the segment height.
Deviation bar charts (bars above and below a zero line): the value is the magnitude, but 'lowest' means most negative, not smallest in size.
q-di-bar.timeTarget: 3:30–4:15 min per 5-question bar set including a 40-second transcription pass. Simple single-bar sets at the fast end; double-bar and stacked sets at the top of the range.
q-di-bar.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you can transcribe a 10-bar double-bar chart into a clean 2×5 table in under 45 seconds with zero legend errors, and finish the 5 questions inside 4 minutes at 4/5 or better — repeated on three consecutive fresh sets.
questionPatterns: Double bar (two years, or two companies) with 'ratio of A in year 1 to B in year 2'.
'In which year was the percentage increase in X over the previous year the highest?'
Stacked bar: 'the share of segment C in 2023 is what percent of the 2023 total?'

'The average of all five bars is what percent of the tallest bar?'
Combo chart: bars for absolute numbers plus a line for a percentage (Mains).
Horizontal bar chart of five branches, questions on differences and ratios.

q-di-line.whatItIs: One or more lines plotted across years or months. Same arithmetic as bar DI, but the question set leans heavily on change, trend and 'between which two years' phrasing.
q-di-line.coreMethod:
1. Read the y-axis interval and the units line exactly as with bars. Write 'one division = ___'.
2. Identify the lines — solid vs dashed, or by marker shape. State the mapping to yourself once.
3. Transcribe every plotted point into a rough-sheet table: years across the top, one row per line. 30-40 seconds. Do not answer from the picture.
4. While transcribing, write the DIFFERENCE between consecutive points underneath the row. It costs five extra seconds and kills half the questions before you read them.
5. For 'percentage increase from year A to year B', base is year A. Write the fraction, cancel, convert with the 1/n table.
6. For 'in which year was the increase maximum', judge by the steepest segment first. If the stem says PERCENTAGE increase, the steepest segment is not automatically the answer — check the two steepest against their own bases.
7. Multi-line sets almost always contain one question about the SUM of both lines in a year and one about the DIFFERENCE. Compute both columns while transcribing.
tricks: Steepness answers absolute-increase questions in three seconds with no arithmetic. Only percentage-increase questions need computation, and then only for the two steepest segments.
'Between which two consecutive years...' has only four candidates in a five-year graph. Eliminate the two visually flat ones instantly and compute two, never four.
Intersection questions ('in which year were sales of A and B equal') are read straight off the crossing point. Zero computation.
Transcribe two lines as two rows aligned by year, so the sum and the difference of each column can be written directly beneath it.
For a six-or-more-point average, add by pairing from the ends inward (first + last, second + second-last) to hit round numbers.
If the y-axis shows a break mark, discard all visual trend impressions and work only from transcribed numbers — the picture is lying by design.
traps: Reading a point between gridlines as an ugly number. Bank DI values are always intended to be clean; if you read 137, it is 135 or 140 and you have misjudged the scale.
'Sales fell by what percent from 2022 to 2023' — base is still 2022. The decreasing case is where base-flipping happens most.
Two lines where one is a percentage and one is an absolute number sharing a single legend box (very common in Mains combo DI).
Assuming values change linearly between plotted points. Questions about an unplotted period are never asked; if a stem seems to ask one, you have misread the axis labels.
'Cumulative' line graphs: each point already includes all previous years, so the value FOR a year is the difference of consecutive points, not the point itself.
Multi-line graphs where a question names a series that does not exist on the chart (a distractor name from the legend of an adjacent set in Mains booklets).
q-di-line.timeTarget: 3:15–4:00 min for a 5-question line set. Single-line sets should finish under 3:30; two-line sets at the top of the range.
q-di-line.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you can answer 'between which two years was the percentage increase highest' on a six-point line graph in under 25 seconds by eliminating to two candidates by eye and computing only those two — and when a two-line transcription is complete and correct within 40 seconds.
questionPatterns: Single line over 5-7 years: average, percentage change, 'highest increase' questions.
Two lines (income and expenditure) where profit = income − expenditure, plus 'in which year was profit percentage highest'.
A line graph of percentage GROWTH RATES rather than absolute values, with one base-year value given — find actual values. This is the hard Mains variant.
'The value in 2024 is what percent of the average of all years?'
Line plus table combination (Mains).
Intersection/equality questions between two series.

q-di-pie.whatItIs: One or two circles split into sectors, labelled either in percentages or in degrees, with a total given in text. The entire topic is: convert once, then treat it as a table.
q-di-pie.coreMethod:
1. Identify the labelling mode immediately — percentages, degrees, or absolute values. Write '%' or '°' at the top of your rough sheet.
2. If the pie is in DEGREES, do not convert every sector. Ratio questions can be answered with degrees directly (they cancel), and value questions use value = (degrees/360) × Total.
3. Write the Total once, boxed, at the top of the sheet. Nearly every question in the set uses it.
4. Convert only the sectors a question actually needs. In a six-sector pie with five questions you typically touch four sectors, never all six twice.
5. Check that the pie sums to 100% (or 360°). If one sector is unlabelled, it is the residual — compute it immediately and write it in, because one question in the set always needs it.
6. For two-pie sets, the single most important line on the page is the text stating whether the two pies share a total or have different totals. Read it before anything else.
7. For cross-pie comparisons, write both as (percentage × total) and simplify the expression before multiplying anything out.
tricks: Degrees stay as degrees for ratios. 'Ratio of A to B' where A = 72° and B = 54° is simply 72:54 = 4:3. Zero conversion, zero total needed.
Memorise the degree anchors: 36° = 10%, 54° = 15%, 72° = 20%, 90° = 25%, 108° = 30%, 120° = 33.33%, 144° = 40%, 180° = 50%. Bank pies are built almost entirely from these.
Difference of two sectors of the SAME pie: compute (a% − b%) first, then one multiplication by the total. Not two multiplications and a subtraction.
'Central angle of sector X' = percentage × 3.6. Run it as ×36 then ÷10.
Two-pie with different totals: compute each pie's 1% value (Total ÷ 100) once and write both at the top. Every later question becomes percentage × that unit.
'What percent of the total is A and B together' — add the percentages and stop. Never compute two absolute values and then divide by the total.
traps: Assuming both pies share the same total when the text gives two different ones — or the reverse, where the text says 'the total of both years together is 12,000' and you must split it.
Percentage of a percentage: 'category A is 25% of the pie, and 40% of category A are girls' means girls are 10% of the total, not 40%.
The unlabelled residual sector. Every pie set has one question needing it and the paper never draws attention to it.

'A is what percent more than B', both from the same pie: the shortcut is (a−b)/b on the raw percentages. Converting to absolutes first wastes 20 seconds; dividing by the TOTAL instead of by b is simply wrong.
A pie labelled in degrees with percentage options (or labelled in percentages with a 'find the central angle' question). Check the units of the OPTIONS, not just the chart.
Percentages that sum to 99 or 101 because of rounding. Do not 'correct' them — use them as printed.
q-di-pie.timeTarget: 3:00–3:45 min for a single-pie 5-question set; 4:00–4:30 for a two-pie set. Pie is the fastest of the four classical DI forms when it appears.
q-di-pie.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when, given a pie in degrees, you answer every ratio question without converting to percentages at all, and you can do 10 mixed degree↔percentage conversions in under 40 seconds with all correct.
questionPatterns: Single pie in percentages with the total given below — absolute values, ratios, differences.
Single pie in degrees — central-angle questions and ratio questions.
Two pies (2022 vs 2023, or 'students' and 'girls among them') with cross-pie comparisons.
Pie plus table combination: the pie gives the split, the table breaks one sector down further (Mains).
'The number in sector A is what percent more than sector D?'
'If 20% of sector B shifted to sector C, what is the new central angle of C?' — the Mains twist.

q-di-caselet.whatItIs: The data is buried in four to eight lines of prose with no chart at all, sometimes with a Venn-diagram flavour. You must construct the table yourself before a single question is answerable.
q-di-caselet.coreMethod:
1. Read the whole paragraph once at normal speed WITHOUT computing anything. You are only establishing: how many entities, how many attributes.
2. Draw the empty grid immediately — entities down the left, attributes across the top. This is the entire game. A tabulated caselet is an easy table DI; a caselet held in your head is unsolvable.
3. Re-read sentence by sentence and fill only the DIRECT values first — any sentence giving an absolute number.
4. Then apply the relational sentences. Convert every percentage relation into a ratio at the moment you read it: '20% more' → 6:5, '25% less' → 3:4, '50% more' → 3:2. Working in ratios keeps decimals out entirely.
5. Use the TOTAL equation last. It is almost always the key that unlocks the final unknown: if everything is expressed in terms of one variable x, the total gives x in a single step.
6. Only after the grid is complete do you read the questions. If the grid cannot be completed, check whether the questions actually need the missing cell — often they do not.
7. Hard rule: if after 90 seconds the grid is less than half full, leave the set. Caselets are the highest-variance DI form and a bad one can eat six minutes.
tricks: Convert every percentage relation to a ratio on sight. 'A is 25% more than B' → A:B = 5:4. This one habit removes almost all the arithmetic from caselets.
Let the SMALLEST quantity be x, not the first one mentioned. Fewer fractions to carry.

Venn-flavoured caselets: draw the circles and fill from the CENTRE outward — the 'all three' number first, then the pairwise 'both' regions, then the singles. Filling from the outside in always produces double counting.
Averages in caselets are disguised totals. 'The average of the five branches is 240' means the total is 1200 — write 1200 and never think about the average again.
Hold the 'total of all = T' sentence back. It is the last usable equation and using it early forces you into simultaneous equations.
Cross out each sentence as you consume it. A bank caselet contains no redundant sentence — if a sentence is left uncrossed at the end, you have missed a constraint and your grid is wrong.
traps: Direction of 'more/less': 'A is 20% less than B' means B is the base (B = 100, A = 80). Reversing this corrupts the entire grid and therefore all five answers.
Nested percentages: '40% of the employees in branch A are women, and 25% of those women are graduates' gives graduate women = 10% of branch A, not 25%.
A name reused in two roles — 'Store A sells shirts and trousers', then a later sentence about 'A' meaning the store, not the shirt line.

Reading the questions first. For CHART DI that is correct; for a caselet it actively wastes time, because the questions are meaningless until the grid exists. This is the one place the general rule inverts.
Venn caselets: '30 play cricket' normally includes those who also play other games. 'Only cricket' is a different, smaller number.
A ratio-derived value coming out as 66.67 or similar. Bank caselets resolve to integers — a non-integer means you have made an error, not that the answer is ugly.
q-di-caselet.timeTarget: 4:30–5:30 min for a 5-question caselet, of which 90-120 seconds is grid building. In Prelims, attempt a caselet only after the other DI set and simplification are finished — often that means not at all.
q-di-caselet.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when your very first physical action on seeing a caselet is drawing an empty grid rather than reading a question, and when on five fresh caselets your grid is complete and fully correct BEFORE you read any question on at least four of them, each within two minutes.
questionPatterns: Two stores or three branches × two or three products, given via percentages and ratios with the grand total supplied in the last sentence.
'In a school there are X students, boys:girls = a:b, of the boys p% play football...' — nested percentage chains.
Venn-style: three sports/subjects/newspapers with 'both', 'all three' and 'only' counts.
A caselet giving a total plus successive relations, with the final question asking for an average or a ratio of two computed values.
Caselet with an arithmetic overlay (Mains): the grid values then feed a profit/loss, SI/CI or time-and-work question.
Caselet where one entity's data is deliberately incomplete and one question is unanswerable-looking but actually needs only the other entities.

q-di-missing.topicName: Data Interpretation — missing value and mixed
q-di-missing.whatItIs: A DI where some cells are blank and text conditions supply what is needed to fill them, or where two different chart types must be read together. Nothing is answerable until you reconstruct the data.
q-di-missing.coreMethod:
1. Count the blanks. Label them x, y, z on the rough sheet.
2. Read the text conditions under the chart and PAIR each condition to exactly one blank before computing anything. Write the pairing.
3. Fill in dependency order: blanks that depend only on printed numbers first; blanks that depend on another blank second. Draw an arrow if the chain is longer than two.
4. Read all 5 stems BEFORE filling. This is the exception to the chart-DI habit — here it decides how much work you do, because typically two of four blanks are decoys that no question touches.
5. For mixed DI (bar + line, table + pie), build ONE unified table combining both sources. Never flick between two charts on a per-question basis.
6. Verify using the total row or column: once the blanks are in, the row must sum to the stated total. This five-second check is the highest-value five seconds in the whole Quant paper.
7. If a blank requires solving a genuine two-variable simultaneous system, the set is above Clerk pay grade for the time available — leave it.
tricks: Fill only what is asked. Reading the stems first typically saves 40-60 seconds because one or two blanks are never used by any question.
Percentage relations for blanks are always clean fractions. Memorise six multipliers: 10% more = ×11/10, 20% more = ×6/5, 25% more = ×5/4, 20% less = ×4/5, 25% less = ×3/4, 50% more = ×3/2.
Free blanks first: if a total is printed and only one cell in that row or column is blank, that blank is a single subtraction. Sweep the grid for these before anything else.
Verification by total costs 5 seconds and protects up to 5 marks. Always run it before you mark a single answer.
In bar+line mixed DI where the line gives a percentage of the bar, compute the actual value once during transcription and write it beside the bar. Do not recompute per question.
When two blanks are linked to each other by a ratio and jointly to a printed total, set the smaller as x and solve one linear equation. Never set up simultaneous equations under an exam clock.
traps: Filling a blank with the percentage relation reversed. This is the single most expensive error in all of DI: one mistake corrupts five answers, costing 5 marks plus 1.25 in penalties.
Assuming a blank is derivable when the condition actually refers to a different row or a different year.
In mixed DI, applying a line-graph percentage to the wrong base — percentage of that year's TOTAL versus percentage of that CATEGORY.
Sets that supply conditions for blanks no question needs, tempting you to spend 90 seconds filling the whole grid.
'The missing value is 20% OF the total' versus '20% MORE THAN the previous year'. The preposition carries the entire meaning; the number is a decoy.
Treating the printed 'Total' as the sum of only the visible cells. It always includes the blanks — that is what makes the free-blank sweep work.
q-di-missing.timeTarget: 5:00–6:00 min for a 5-question missing-value set. This is the slowest DI form there is. In Prelims it should be your last DI attempt or an outright skip; in Mains, where marks decide merit, it is worth the time.

questionPatterns: Table with 3-4 blanks plus text conditions such as 'the number sold in 2023 was 20% more than in 2022'.

A set where the last question asks for a value that requires a blank you were never given enough information to fill — the intended answer is derived from a total instead.

q-di-arith.whatItIs: A chart wrapped around an arithmetic chapter. The chart supplies the numbers, but each question is really a profit-and-loss, SI/CI, time-and-work, boats-and-streams, partnership or mixture problem.
q-di-arith.coreMethod:
1. Identify the underlying arithmetic chapter from the COLUMN HEADERS before reading a single question. 'CP / No. of articles / Profit%' = profit and loss. 'Principal / Rate / Time' = interest. 'Men / Days / Work' = time and work. 'Speed of boat / Speed of stream' = boats and streams. 'Investment / Months' = partnership.
2. Write the governing formula at the top of your rough sheet ONCE, before any question: Profit% = (SP−CP)/CP×100; SI = PRT/100; CI−SI for 2 years = P(r/100)²; M1×D1/W1 = M2×D2/W2; downstream = b+s, upstream = b−s; profit share ∝ capital × time.
3. Transcribe the chart into a table exactly as with any other DI.
4. Per question, the only decision is which formula variable is unknown. Write the formula, substitute, solve. Do not improvise a route.
5. Prefer ratio and unit methods over formula methods. For time and work, take total work = LCM of the days and convert everyone to units per day. For profit, work with the CP:SP ratio.
6. Chain percentages multiplicatively, never additively: a 25% markup followed by a 20% discount is ×5/4 × ×4/5 = ×1 — no profit, no loss.
7. For CI at standard rates over 2 years use fixed multipliers: 5% → 1.1025, 10% → 1.21, 20% → 1.44. Memorise these three plus the 3-year 10% factor 1.331.
tricks: Cancelling percentage pairs: markup 25% then discount 20% cancels exactly; markup 20% then discount 16.67% cancels exactly; markup 50% then discount 33.33% cancels exactly. Recognising one of these answers a whole question in five seconds.
CI − SI for two years = P(r/100)². The most-asked interest question in bank DI, answerable in about ten seconds.
Time and work by LCM units: A in 12 days, B in 18 days → total work 36 units, A = 3/day, B = 2/day. Every subsequent question becomes a division. Never touch 1/12 + 1/18.
Efficiency is inversely proportional to time: '20% more efficient' means time is ×5/6, not ×6/5. Write this on your formula card — it is the most-missed relation in the topic.
Partnership from a DI table: compute the three (capital × time) products once, reduce the ratio once, and every share question is one multiplication.

Where a chart value takes three steps to extract and the option gaps are wide, approximate the CHART value but keep the FORMULA step exact. Precision belongs where the formula is, not where the reading is.
traps: Applying the SI formula because the column header says 'rate of interest' when the stem says 'compounded annually'. The chapter is decided by the STEM, not the chart.
Computing profit percent on SP instead of CP. Profit% is always on CP unless the question explicitly says otherwise — and if it does, it says so in words you must not skim past.
Discount is on MARKED price while profit is on COST price. A chart giving both MP and CP exists specifically to make you use the wrong base.
Mixing the chart's unit (in thousands) into a rupee formula without scaling — then getting an answer 1000× off and picking the nearest option anyway.
Half-yearly or quarterly compounding: halve the rate and double the time (or quarter and ×4). One word in the stem, two changes to the formula.
In boats-and-streams DI, reading 'speed in still water' as 'downstream speed'. Downstream = b + s; the chart usually gives b and s separately so you must add.
q-di-arith.timeTarget: 5:00–6:30 min for a 5-question arithmetic DI set in Mains (60-75 sec/question). Acceptable in Mains where the set is worth 5 questions of a merit-deciding paper; too slow for Prelims unless everything else is done.
q-di-arith.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you can name the underlying arithmetic chapter within 10 seconds of seeing the column headers, write its formula without hesitation, and clear 4 of 5 questions inside 6 minutes on three consecutive fresh sets. Secondary check: you can state CI−SI for 2 years as P(r/100)² and the efficiency-time inverse relation from memory, cold.
questionPatterns: Table of CP, number of articles and profit% per shop → find SP, total profit, and cross-shop comparisons.
Bar chart of principal amounts plus a table of rates → SI versus CI comparisons, and CI−SI questions.
Table of men, days and work completed → 'how many additional men are needed to finish in X days'.

q-di-new.topicName: Data Interpretation — new patterns: radar, funnel, scatter, sunburst (Mains)
q-di-new.whatItIs: Unfamiliar chart shapes carrying entirely ordinary data. The novelty is cosmetic and the arithmetic is usually lighter than a caselet. What is actually being tested is whether you panic.
q-di-new.coreMethod:
1. Recognise the family within five seconds:
   • RADAR / web / spider — axes radiating from a centre, one polygon per series. Each axis is a category; distance from the centre is the value.
   • FUNNEL — stacked horizontal bands narrowing downward, representing a stage-wise process (applied → shortlisted → interviewed → selected). Values shrink down the funnel.
   • SCATTER / X-Y — each labelled point carries two coordinates; read (x, y) per point.
   • SUNBURST — concentric rings, inner ring is the parent category, outer ring subdivides it. Read the inner ring first, always.
   • STOCK / candlestick — four numbers per period: open, high, low, close.
2. Convert to a table immediately. This is the entire technique. Every one of these charts reduces to a 5×3 grid inside 45 seconds.
3. RADAR: categories as columns, series as rows. Check the scale marks along one axis and confirm the same scale applies to all axes.
4. FUNNEL: also write the DROP between consecutive stages while transcribing, because conversion-rate questions are the whole set.
5. SUNBURST: write the parent value and each child's share, then confirm the children sum to the parent. If they do not, the outer ring is a percentage of the parent rather than an absolute.
6. SCATTER: tabulate name, x and y. Questions are almost always about the ratio y/x or 'which point has the highest y per x'.
7. Once tabulated, apply the table-DI method unchanged.
tricks: The 45-second tabulation rule: never answer any question directly off a novel chart. Tabulate first and it becomes a table you have already practised a hundred times.
Funnel overall conversion: do not multiply three stage percentages. Compute final stage ÷ first stage directly — one division instead of three multiplications.
Sunburst outer rings are normally percentages OF THEIR PARENT, not of the grand total. Establish this in the first 15 seconds; it determines every single answer in the set.
Radar with two polygons: 'in how many categories did A exceed B' is answered by seeing which polygon lies outside on each axis. Five seconds, no numbers at all.
Scatter 'highest ratio' questions: mentally sweep a line from the origin — the point requiring the steepest line wins. Confirm only the top two numerically.

These sets are deliberately placed to intimidate. If you tabulate calmly, they are frequently the EASIEST five marks in the Mains section, because the setters keep the arithmetic light to compensate for the unfamiliar presentation.
traps: Applying a sunburst outer-ring percentage to the grand total instead of to its parent segment. This is the defining error of the format.
Radar charts where one axis carries its own scale (rare, but when it happens it is the entire trick of the set). Check every axis label, not just one.
Funnel: reading a band's WIDTH as its value when the value is printed inside the band; or assuming each stage is a percentage of the previous when the numbers are absolute (or the reverse).
Scatter: swapping x and y in a ratio question. Write the axis labels on your table, not just the numbers.
Spending 90 seconds studying the chart because it is interesting or alarming. The novelty is the trap; the arithmetic is not.
Skipping the set on sight because it looks hard. In Mains this is often the most gettable set on the page, and skipping it is a decision made by fear rather than by marks-per-minute.
q-di-new.timeTarget: 4:30–5:30 min per 5-question set including a 45-second tabulation. Target no slower than your table-DI time plus one minute — if you are consistently slower than that, the problem is tabulation speed, not arithmetic.
q-di-new.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you can look at a radar, funnel, scatter or sunburst chart you have never seen before and produce a correct rough-sheet table within 45 seconds — and when your accuracy on new-pattern sets sits within 10 percentage points of your accuracy on plain table DI.
questionPatterns: Radar chart of five products across two years → ratios, percentage change, 'in how many products did 2023 exceed 2022'.
Funnel of a recruitment or sales pipeline → stage-to-stage conversion percentages, overall conversion, 'how many were lost at stage 3'.
Scatter of runs versus matches, or marks versus students → averages and highest-ratio questions.
Sunburst of a company's departments with a male/female split in the outer ring → nested percentage questions.
Stock/candlestick chart → range (high − low), percentage change from open to close.

q-series-missing.whatItIs: Five or six numbers with one replaced by a blank. Find the pattern, supply the term. Pure pattern recognition with no arithmetic depth — and completely all-or-nothing.
q-series-missing.coreMethod:
1. Compute first differences across the whole series before theorising about anything. Write them in the gaps.
2. Read the differences:
   • constant → arithmetic series
   • differences themselves patterned (2, 4, 6, 8 or 3, 6, 12, 24) → second-level series
   • differences are squares (1, 4, 9, 16), cubes (1, 8, 27, 64) or primes (2, 3, 5, 7, 11) → the standard bank families
3. If the differences are chaotic, switch to RATIOS — divide consecutive terms. A ratio near 2, 3 or 1.5, or one growing steadily, means multiplicative.
4. Run the bank templates in this order; they cover roughly 85% of what IBPS asks:
   a. ×2+1, ×2−1, ×3+2 (multiply then add a small constant)
   b. ×0.5, ×1.5, ×2.5, ×3.5 — increasing half-integer multipliers, extremely common and invisible to the difference method
   c. +n², +n³, or ±(n × constant)
   d. previous term + (difference multiplied by a growing factor)
   e. n²±n, n³±n
   f. sum of the two previous terms
   g. alternating — two interleaved patterns
5. If the series has six or more terms and nothing appears within 20 seconds, split it: check 1st/3rd/5th and 2nd/4th/6th separately.
6. VERIFY your rule on at least two terms other than the one that suggested it. A rule confirmed on a single gap is a guess.
7. Hard 30-second rule: no pattern in 30 seconds, move on. Series gives no partial credit and offers no reliable way to narrow the options.
tricks: The ×0.5 / ×1.5 / ×2.5 / ×3.5 family: whenever terms grow but the ratio is between 1 and 3 and not constant, test increasing half-integer multipliers. This single family accounts for a large share of bank series and is completely invisible if you only look at differences.
Three-second growth diagnosis: slow growth then explosion = multiplicative; steady growth = additive. Decide first, then run ONE test instead of two.

Squares to 30 and cubes to 15 on instant recall. Most 'hidden' series are a square or cube offset by 1 or 2: 122 = 11²+1, 217 = 6³+1, 730 = 9³+1. If a term sits one or two away from a clean power, that is the pattern.
Any decimal or fractional term means multiplier series. Start with ratios, never with differences.
When the blank is early in the series, work backwards from the last terms — the later terms usually display the pattern most clearly because the increments are largest.
Use the options for magnitude, not precision. If your rule predicts around 380 and the options are 240, 260, 384, 410, take 384 and move — do not verify to the last digit.
traps: Forcing a difference pattern onto a multiplicative series. This is the biggest time sink in the topic: give differences 15 seconds, then switch unconditionally.
Ignoring the first term. Many series only reveal themselves at term 1 → term 2, especially the ×0.5-then-×1-then-×1.5 family.
Assuming the multiplier stays constant when the multiplier is itself the pattern.
Mis-copying a digit from the screen to the rough sheet. The series then becomes genuinely unsolvable and you will spend 90 seconds blaming the pattern instead of re-reading.
Spending 90 seconds because you are 'almost there'. Under a 20-minute sectional clock, 90 seconds is three or four simplification questions — an objectively terrible trade.
Reading an alternating series as a single sequence. If the terms go up-down-up-down, split them immediately.
q-series-missing.timeTarget: 30-40 seconds per question, hard cap 45 seconds. A five-question series block should be finished inside 3 minutes or partially abandoned.
q-series-missing.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you can name the pattern FAMILY (additive / multiplicative / alternating / square-cube) within 10 seconds on 9 of 10 fresh series, and complete a 5-question set in under 3 minutes with at least 4 correct. q-series-wrong.whatItIs: A complete series is printed and exactly one term breaks the pattern. Identify it. Harder than missing-term because you must establish the rule from terms you cannot fully trust.
q-series-wrong.coreMethod:
1. Assume the FIRST and LAST terms are correct and build the rule forward from term 1. Bank papers essentially never plant the error at either end, and when they do the break is unmistakable.
2. Generate the series yourself from term 1 using your candidate rule, writing your PREDICTED values in a row ABOVE the printed ones.
3. The first mismatch is your answer — but confirm the rule continues correctly AFTER the mismatch using the printed values. The following term should follow the pattern from the CORRECT value, not from the wrong one. This is what distinguishes a genuinely wrong term from a wrong rule.
4. If your rule breaks in two places, the rule is wrong, not the series. Restart with a different family. Exactly one term is ever wrong.
5. Where the pattern is second-level, write two rows of differences — a single wrong term shows up as one clear spike.
6. Read the stem word: the answer is the WRONG TERM unless the question says 'what should come in its place', in which case it is the CORRECTED value. The option list usually contains both.
tricks: Predict-forward rather than diagnose-backward. Writing your own predicted series above the printed one exposes the error in a single glance instead of forcing you through five hypotheses.
The wrong term is usually 'close but not clean'. If a series is built on squares and one term is 145 while 144 = 12², that term is the answer. Look for the value sitting 1-3 away from a clean power.

The paired-difference signature: in an additive second-level series a single wrong term produces TWO adjacent bad differences — one too large and one too small by the same amount. That signature confirms the answer instantly with no further checking.
Never doubt a beautiful pattern because of one term. If differences run 6, 12, 24, 48, 97, then 97 is wrong because 96 fits. The term that breaks the elegance IS the answer.
Once found, do not re-verify the whole series. Confirm only the two terms adjacent to the suspect and move on.
Mains wrong-term series lean heavily on the x0.5 / x1.5 / x2.5 family with decimals. Any decimal anywhere means test multipliers before differences.
traps: Declaring a term wrong when the pattern legitimately shifts there by design (the multiplier itself increments at that point). Always verify beyond the suspect term.
Being asked for the wrong term and marking the corrected value, or vice versa. Both appear in the options, deliberately.
Building your rule from terms 2 and 3 when term 2 is the wrong one. Start from term 1, always.
Persisting with a difference approach on a multiplicative series — same trap as missing-term series, but costlier here because the printed sequence gives you more terms to waste time on.
Correcting more than one term to make a rule work. If your rule needs two corrections, discard the rule.
Assuming the wrong term must be visually odd (much larger or smaller). It is usually within a few percent of the correct value.
q-series-wrong.timeTarget: 40-50 seconds per question, hard cap 60 seconds. Marginally slower than missing-term because you must generate the whole predicted series.
q-series-wrong.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you find the wrong term by writing a predicted series above the printed one rather than by testing hypotheses one at a time, and clear 4 of 5 in under 4 minutes on fresh sets. Objective check: across 10 fresh questions you never once mark the corrected value when the stem asked for the wrong term.
questionPatterns: Six-term series with one wrong term; the options are the printed terms themselves.
'Which value should replace the wrong term?' — the options are corrected values.
Series where consecutive differences are squares or cubes and exactly one is off by 1.
Multiplier series with a decimal multiplier where one term has been rounded incorrectly.
Two series presented together following the same rule, with the error in one of them (Mains variant).
Series where the wrong term is the SECOND term, punishing anyone who built the rule from terms 2 and 3.

q-quadratic.whatItIs: Two equations in x and y; determine the relation between them (x > y, x < y, x ≥ y, x ≤ y, x = y, or no relation). The whole topic is factorisation speed plus one comparison discipline.
q-quadratic.coreMethod:
1. For ax² + bx + c = 0 with a = 1: find two numbers that MULTIPLY to c and ADD to b. The roots are the NEGATIVES of that pair. Say it as a fixed rule: 'roots = minus the pair'. For x² − 7x + 12 = 0 the pair is (−3, −4), so the roots are 3 and 4.
2. Sign shortcut — memorise this and stop factorising blindly:
   • c positive, b positive → both roots negative
   • c positive, b negative → both roots positive
   • c negative → the roots have opposite signs
   This gives you the sign of both roots before any computation, and often ends the question on its own.
3. When a ≠ 1: multiply a×c, split b into two numbers whose product is a×c, then divide each by a. For 2x² + 7x + 6: a×c = 12, split 7 into 3 and 4, roots = −3/2 and −2.
4. Compare with the FOUR-CORNER method. Write x's two roots and y's two roots, then compare every x-root against every y-root — four comparisons.
   • all four give x > y → answer is x > y
   • all four consistent with at least one equality → x ≥ y (or ≤)
   • any mixed direction → no relation
5. Never skip the four-corner check. Comparing only the larger roots is the single most common error in this topic.
6. For linear-system questions (3x + 2y = 14 and 2x + 3y = 11), just solve the system — 30 seconds — then compare the two values directly.
7. If a discriminant is not a perfect square, the roots are irrational and the answer is almost always 'cannot be determined'. Check and move.
tricks: Sign rule before factorisation: if both x-roots are positive and both y-roots are negative, the answer is x > y in about eight seconds with no factorisation at all.

Range comparison instead of four comparisons: if x's roots are {3, 4} and y's are {5, 6}, the ranges do not overlap so x < y immediately. If the ranges overlap at all, the answer is 'no relation'. Same result, half the work.

Recognise products of consecutive integers. c values of 12, 20, 30, 42, 56, 72, 90 split as (3,4), (4,5), (5,6), (6,7), (7,8), (8,9), (9,10). Bank setters reuse these constantly, so the split is instant.
A difference of squares (x² = 49) gives roots ±7. Roots of opposite sign almost always produce 'no relation' — check the other equation's range and finish.
When both root pairs sit on the same side of zero, 'no relation' is a poor guess. When the ranges overlap, 'no relation' is the most likely answer. Use this if you must guess.
The shape 'x² = 144, y = 12' appears constantly. The answer is x ≤ y (because x can be −12 or +12), NOT x = y.
traps: Comparing only the largest roots. With x ∈ {2, 9} and y ∈ {4, 5}, only the four-corner check reveals that the correct answer is 'no relation'.
Confusing 'no relation can be established' with 'x = y'. These are different options and both are always present.
Sign errors in factorisation: x² + 5x + 6 has roots −2 and −3, not +2 and +3. The sign rule exists specifically to prevent this.
Forgetting to divide by a when a ≠ 1, producing roots that are a-times too large.
Solving for y first and then reading the option list, which is always phrased as x relative to y. Inverting the relation at the last step throws away a correct solution.
The ≥ and ≤ options: if one x-root equals one y-root and every other comparison points the same way, the answer is ≥ or ≤, never >. Papers include this deliberately and it is the most-missed variant.
q-quadratic.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per question. A 5-question block should be done in under 2 minutes 30 seconds. When it appears, this is the fastest-scoring topic in the entire Quant paper.
q-quadratic.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you can factorise any bank-level quadratic with a = 1 in under 8 seconds, state the signs of both roots from b and c alone without factorising, and clear a 5-question block in under 2 minutes 30 seconds at 5/5 — repeated on three consecutive sets.
questionPatterns: Two standard quadratics, find the relation between x and y. The staple.
One quadratic and one linear equation.
Two simultaneous linear equations in x and y, then compare.
Inequality form: 'I. x² − 11x + 30 = 0, II. y² − 15y + 56 = 0'.
Equations written with terms rearranged ('12 + x² = 7x') purely to slow your pattern recognition.
Mains variant with surds or square roots, e.g. √x = 4 and y² = 16 — where √x is defined as the positive root only, so x = 16 and y = ±4, giving x ≥ y.

q-quantity.topicName: Quantity I vs Quantity II comparison (Mains)
q-quantity.whatItIs: Two independent word problems labelled Quantity I and Quantity II; compute both and state the relation. Effectively two arithmetic questions for one mark — the worst marks-per-minute ratio in the paper.
q-quantity.coreMethod:
1. Read BOTH quantities before solving either. Decide which is faster and do that one first. If Quantity I is a three-step time-and-work problem and Quantity II is a one-line percentage, do II first.
2. Identify the arithmetic chapter for each quantity independently. They are normally from different chapters and share nothing.
3. Apply the ESTIMATE-FIRST GATE: round both to one significant figure in about 15 seconds. If the estimates differ by more than roughly 20%, the relation is settled and you skip exact computation entirely.
4. If the estimates are close, solve exactly — not approximately. The options are relations, so a near-miss produces a wrong relation and a full penalty.
5. If either quantity resists in 40 seconds, abandon the question. Do not solve one and guess the other.
6. Watch for a 'cannot be determined' option, which exists whenever one quantity has insufficient data — roughly one question in eight.
7. The three-quantity ordering variant appears in Mains. Solve all three, then order them. Attempt it only if all three are single-step.
tricks: The estimate-first gate settles roughly 40% of these questions with no exact computation at all. It is the single highest-value habit in the topic.

Do the cheap quantity first. If it produces a very large or very small value, the expensive quantity can often be BOUNDED rather than computed — you only need to know which side of the cheap value it falls on.

Recognise the standard pairings IBPS uses: average vs percentage, SI vs CI, speed-time vs time-work, probability vs a plain fraction. Naming the pairing tells you both formulas before you have read carefully.
If both quantities reduce to the SAME formula with different inputs (two SI computations at the same rate), compare the inputs directly — compare P×T rather than computing two interest amounts.
'Quantity I: value of x in [equation]. Quantity II: value of y in [equation]' is a disguised quadratic comparison. Switch to the four-corner method immediately.
Never leave a Quantity question half-solved. Either both quantities or neither. A half-solved question scores zero and has already cost you a minute.
traps: Solving Quantity I and then guessing Quantity II because the clock ran out. That is a 0.25 penalty with a one-in-five upside — strictly negative expected value after you have already spent the time.
Unit mismatch between the two quantities (Quantity I in km/h, Quantity II in m/s) and comparing the raw numbers.
Missing the ≥ and ≤ options. Read the option list before deciding, because some papers offer '=' and others offer '≥' for the same situation.
Assuming the two quantities are connected. They are entirely independent problems and nothing carries from I into II.
Attempting this block early in Mains Quant. It has the worst marks-per-minute ratio in the section and belongs at the end.
Reading 'Quantity I ≥ Quantity II' and 'Quantity I > Quantity II' as the same option under time pressure.
q-quantity.timeTarget: 70-90 seconds per question honestly — it is two problems for one mark. With the estimate-first gate the best cases fall to 40 seconds. Past 100 seconds, abandon without regret.
q-quantity.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when the estimate-first gate is automatic and settles at least 2 of every 5 Quantity questions without exact computation, and when you never exceed 100 seconds on a single question. Objective test: a 5-question Quantity block completed in under 6 minutes total with 4 or more correct.
questionPatterns: Quantity I a time-and-work problem, Quantity II a percentage or profit problem.
Quantity I simple interest on a principal, Quantity II compound interest on the same or a different principal.
Quantity I the value of x from a quadratic, Quantity II the value of y from another — a disguised quadratic comparison.
Quantity I a probability, Quantity II a plain numeric fraction.
The three-quantity ordering variant (arrange Quantity I, II and III).
A quantity stated with genuinely insufficient data, making 'cannot be determined' correct.

q-ds.whatItIs: A question plus two (occasionally three) statements; decide which statements are SUFFICIENT to answer it — without actually answering. The entire discipline is: do not solve.
q-ds.coreMethod:
1. Read the question stem and write down exactly what is asked and what would be needed to answer it. 'Find the speed of the train' → I need distance and time, or speed via some other relation.
2. Cover statement II with your hand. Ask: does I ALONE answer it? Write 'I: Y' or 'I: N'.
3. Cover statement I. Ask: does II ALONE answer it? Write 'II: Y' or 'II: N'.
4. Only if both are N do you ask whether I and II TOGETHER answer it.
5. Map to the option letters. Read the instruction block ONCE at the start of the section and then trust it — the standard shape is: (a) I alone sufficient but II alone not, (b) II alone sufficient but I alone not, (c) either alone sufficient, (d) neither alone nor together sufficient, (e) both together needed. The lettering does vary between papers, which is exactly why you read it once, carefully, at the start.
6. Never compute the answer. You only need to establish that a UNIQUE answer exists. Set up the equations, count unknowns against independent equations, stop.
7. Counting rule: n unknowns require n independent equations. A statement that restates information you already have adds nothing, however differently it is phrased.
tricks: Count equations instead of solving them. 'Find the two-digit number. I: the sum of the digits is 9. II: the number is divisible by 4.' Do not hunt for the number — establish how many candidates each statement leaves.

Uniqueness, not existence. A statement that leads to a quadratic with TWO valid positive roots is INSUFFICIENT, because two answers are possible. This is the single most-tested subtlety in bank DS — always ask 'one answer or two?'

Physical-constraint rejection: if a quadratic gives roots 5 and −3 and the quantity is a number of people, a length or an age, the negative root is rejected and the statement IS sufficient. Check the physical constraint before declaring insufficiency.

Ratios alone are NEVER sufficient for an absolute quantity, and ALWAYS sufficient for another ratio. Ratio plus one absolute value is sufficient. This one rule answers a large fraction of bank DS on sight.

If both statements say the same thing in different words — 'the ratio of A to B is 3:5' and 'B is 66.67% more than A' — the answer is 'either alone'. Papers hide identical information behind different phrasings specifically to test this.
Statements I and II are always individually TRUE. If they appear to contradict each other, you have misread one of them — never resolve a contradiction, re-read instead.
traps: Solving the problem. It costs 60+ seconds per question and earns nothing, because DS awards no marks for the answer itself.
Carrying information from statement I into your evaluation of statement II. Each must be evaluated in complete isolation — this is what the hand-covering step is physically for.
Declaring 'sufficient' when the statement yields two possible values.
Misreading the option code, particularly when a paper mixes two-statement and three-statement questions with different lettering conventions.
In the three-statement variant, forgetting to test the 'any two of the three' combinations before concluding all three are needed.
Assuming a geometry DS question needs a diagram. It never does — the data is always sufficient to determine sufficiency without drawing.
q-ds.timeTarget: 35-45 seconds per question. DS is among the fastest Mains topics IF you refuse to solve. If you catch yourself computing, you have already lost the time budget for that question.
q-ds.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you can answer a DS question having written no arithmetic at all — only 'I: Y/N, II: Y/N' — on at least 8 of 10 questions, and complete a 5-question DS block in under 3 minutes 30 seconds with 4 or more correct.
questionPatterns: Two-statement standard: 'What is the speed of the boat in still water? I: ... II: ...'
Three-statement variant asking which of the three statements are needed.
Age problems ('What is A's present age?') — the classic DS shape, usually solvable by equation counting alone.
Percentage or profit DS where one statement supplies a ratio and the other an absolute value.
Time-and-work DS where one statement gives a combined efficiency.
Geometry DS: area of a rectangle given the perimeter plus one relation between the sides.
A DS question where a statement leads to a quadratic with two valid positive roots — the insufficiency trap.

q-mensuration-2d.whatItIs: Areas and perimeters of squares, rectangles, triangles, circles and the composite figures built from them. In bank exams it arrives inside word problems and arithmetic DI far more often than as pure geometry.
q-mensuration-2d.coreMethod:
1. Have these on instant recall — this IS the topic:
   • Rectangle: A = l×b, P = 2(l+b), diagonal = √(l²+b²)
   • Square: A = a², P = 4a, diagonal = a√2, and A = d²/2
   • Circle: A = πr², C = 2πr — use π = 22/7 whenever the radius is a multiple of 7, otherwise 3.14
   • Triangle: A = ½ × base × height; equilateral A = (√3/4)a², height = (√3/2)a
   • Right triangle: A = ½ × the two legs
   • Parallelogram: A = base × height. Rhombus: A = ½ d₁d₂
   • Trapezium: A = ½(a+b)×h
   • Semicircle: A = πr²/2, PERIMETER = πr + 2r
   • Sector: A = (θ/360)πr², arc = (θ/360)×2πr
2. Draw the figure. Always, even for a rectangle. A ten-second sketch prevents the commonest error, which is losing track of which dimension is which.
3. Label every given number on the sketch immediately, including units.
4. For composite figures, decompose into standard shapes and write the whole sum-or-difference EXPRESSION before computing any single number.
5. Scaling rule: if a linear dimension scales by k, the area scales by k². 'The side of a square is increased by 20%' → area ×(1.2)² = ×1.44 → up 44%. This one rule answers an entire class of questions in ten seconds.
6. Keep π symbolic until the final step — in comparison and ratio questions it cancels entirely.
7. Path and border problems: outer area minus inner area, where the outer dimensions are (l + 2w) and (b + 2w). Write both outer dimensions before computing anything.
tricks: Percentage change in area in one line: length +a%, breadth +b% → area change = a + b + ab/100. Length +20%, breadth −10% → 20 − 10 − 2 = +8%. No areas computed at all.
π = 22/7 whenever a 7 appears in the radius or the options contain sevenths. The paper is signalling which value to use.

Pythagorean triples on sight: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25), (9,40,41) and their multiples (6,8,10), (9,12,15), (10,24,26), (15,20,25). Recognising one removes a square-root computation entirely.
Square from its diagonal: A = d²/2. Faster than finding the side first, and it appears constantly.
Learn √2 ≈ 1.414 and √3 ≈ 1.732 to three decimals. Those two numbers are all the irrationals a bank paper ever needs.
If a circle and a square have equal PERIMETERS, the circle always has the greater AREA. Answers 'which is greater' questions with zero computation.
traps: Perimeter versus area in the stem — read whether the given number describes a boundary (fencing, wire, cost per metre) or a surface (turfing, tiling, cost per square metre).
Unit conversion in area is SQUARED: 1 m² = 10,000 cm². Dimensions given in cm with options in m² is a standard bank setup.
Diameter supplied where the formula wants radius. Bank papers give the diameter deliberately and frequently.
Semicircle perimeter is πr + 2r, not πr. The straight diameter edge is part of the boundary.
Applying an 'area increases by x%' percentage to the linear dimension instead of using the k² rule.
A path AROUND a rectangle adds 2w to each dimension, not w — the path runs along both opposite sides.
q-mensuration-2d.timeTarget: 45-60 seconds per question for a standard word problem, up to 90 seconds for a composite figure. In Prelims mensuration usually appears as a single arithmetic question, so budget 60 seconds and skip if the figure is composite.
q-mensuration-2d.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you can write all 12 core formulas from memory in under 3 minutes with zero errors, and answer any 'dimension changed by x%, find the change in area' question in under 15 seconds using a + b + ab/100 without computing a single actual area.
questionPatterns: 'The length of a rectangle is increased by 20% and the breadth reduced by 10%. Find the percentage change in area.'
'The area of a square equals the area of a circle of radius 14 cm. Find the perimeter of the square.' — cross-shape linkage.
A path or road around a rectangular garden, with the cost of gravelling at Rs x per square metre.
A circle inscribed in a square, or a square inscribed in a circle — find the shaded area.
Perimeter of a semicircular field and the cost of fencing it.
Mensuration values supplied by a DI table (Mains arithmetic DI).
Equilateral triangle area from its perimeter.

q-mensuration-3d.whatItIs: Volumes and surface areas of cuboid, cube, cylinder, cone, sphere and hemisphere, plus the melted-and-recast family that dominates the topic in bank exams.
q-mensuration-3d.coreMethod:
1. Formulas on instant recall:
   • Cuboid: V = lbh, TSA = 2(lb+bh+hl), diagonal = √(l²+b²+h²)
   • Cube: V = a³, TSA = 6a², diagonal = a√3
   • Cylinder: V = πr²h, CSA = 2πrh, TSA = 2πr(r+h)
   • Cone: V = ⅓πr²h, CSA = πrl, TSA = πr(r+l), slant l = √(r²+h²)
   • Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³, SA = 4πr²
   • Hemisphere: V = (2/3)πr³, CSA = 2πr², TSA = 3πr²
2. Classify in five seconds: (a) direct formula, (b) melting/recasting, (c) ratio or scaling, (d) rate problem (water filling or emptying a tank).
3. MELTING AND RECASTING: volume is conserved. Write V₁ = V₂ and cancel π and every common factor BEFORE computing. Almost every 3D bank question is this single line.
4. Scaling rule: linear ×k → surface area ×k², volume ×k³. 'The radius is doubled' → volume ×8.
5. Rate problems: volume ÷ rate = time. Watch the units — flow in litres per minute against a tank in cubic metres.
6. For a cone, sphere and cylinder sharing the same radius and height, V_cone : V_sphere : V_cylinder = 1 : 2 : 3. Learn this ratio; it answers a whole question type instantly.
7. Keep π symbolic to the final step. In every recasting problem it cancels.
tricks: Cancel π first, always. In a melting problem, (4/3)πR³ = n × (4/3)πr³ collapses to n = (R/r)³ in one line with no arithmetic at all.
Number of small spheres from a big sphere = (R/r)³. Number of small cubes from a big cube = (A/a)³. No formula needed beyond the cube of the ratio.
Learn cubes to 15 and recognise the standard recasting answers: 1728 = 12³, 2744 = 14³, 3375 = 15³, 4096 = 16³. Recasting answers are almost always perfect cubes.
When a cylinder's r and h are given as a ratio, express both via one variable x. Volume becomes a constant × x³ — one unknown, one equation, one cube root.

A rectangular sheet rolled into a cylinder: the joined side's length becomes the circumference (2πr), the other side becomes the height. The stem always specifies which side is joined — that one word decides the whole problem.
A well or pit dug and the earth spread over a field: volume of the cylinder (or cuboid) = area of field × rise in level. One equation, every time.
traps: Curved surface area versus total surface area. 'The cost of painting the outer surface of a CLOSED cylindrical tank' is TSA; 'the label wrapped around a tin' is CSA. One adjective changes the formula.

Cone slant height versus vertical height. CSA uses the slant l, volume uses the vertical h. The question gives one and expects you to derive the other by Pythagoras — and the wrong-value option is always present.
Hemisphere TSA (3πr²) includes the flat circular face; CSA (2πr²) does not. Read whether the object is a solid hemisphere or a bowl.
Volume unit conversion is CUBED: 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³ = 1000 litres. This appears in nearly every tank problem.
Equating SURFACE AREAS instead of volumes in a recasting problem. Melting conserves volume, never surface.
Diameter given where radius is required — the same deliberate setup as in 2D, and doubly costly here because the error is cubed.
q-mensuration-3d.timeTarget: 60-75 seconds per question. Recasting questions with clean numbers should land under 45 seconds once π is cancelled.
q-mensuration-3d.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you can write all 15 volume and surface-area formulas from memory in under 4 minutes with zero errors, and solve any 'melted and recast into n smaller pieces' question in under 40 seconds by cancelling π and taking a cube ratio.

q-permutation.whatItIs: Counting arrangements (order matters) and selections (order does not). At Clerk level the questions are shallow — the real difficulty is deciding which of the two you are looking at.
q-permutation.coreMethod:
1. Make the ONE decision first: does changing the ORDER create a different outcome?
   • Yes — seating, ranking, forming words, forming numbers, prizes that differ → PERMUTATION, nPr = n!/(n−r)!
   • No — committees, teams, handshakes, drawing balls, choosing subjects → COMBINATION, nCr = n!/(r!(n−r)!)
   Write 'P' or 'C' on the rough sheet before computing anything.
2. Compute nCr the fast way, never with full factorials: nCr = (n × (n−1) × ... r terms) ÷ (r × (r−1) × ... × 1). So 10C3 = (10×9×8)/(3×2×1) = 120.
3. Use the identity nCr = nC(n−r). 12C10 becomes 12C2 = 66. This is the single biggest time-saver in the topic and turns an ugly computation into a trivial one.
4. Conditional committee problems ('at least 2 women'): break into cases, compute each with nCr, then ADD. Cases joined by OR are added; sub-choices within a case joined by AND are multiplied. Write 'OR = +, AND = ×' at the top of your sheet.
5. 'At least one' problems: use TOTAL − NONE. Always faster than summing cases.
6. Word arrangements: total letters factorial ÷ the factorial of each repeated letter's count. ARRANGE (7 letters, A×2, R×2) = 7!/(2!·2!) = 1260.
7. 'Vowels together': treat the vowel block as one unit, arrange the units, then arrange within the block, and multiply.
8. Circular arrangement: (n−1)! around a round table; (n−1)!/2 for a garland or necklace where reflections are identical.
tricks: nCr = nC(n−r) — always convert to the smaller r before computing. 15C13 becomes 15C2 = 105.
Memorise the small values: nC1 = n, nC0 = nCn = 1, and nC2 = n(n−1)/2. For n = 5 to 12, nC2 runs 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55, 66. These appear constantly in handshake and 'select 2' questions.
Cancel before multiplying: in (10×9×8)/(3×2×1), cancel the 9 against the 3 and the 8 against the 2 first. Never compute the full numerator.
'At least' → complement. 'At least one girl in a team of 3 chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls' = 9C3 − 5C3 = 84 − 10 = 74. Three tokens of work instead of three cases.

The handshake formula nC2 is also the answer for 'number of lines through n points', 'number of diagonals plus sides in an n-gon' and 'number of matches in a single round robin'. One formula, four question types.
traps: Committee versus seating. 'In how many ways can 3 people be SELECTED' is C; 'SEATED in a row' is P; 'given first, second and third prize' is P. This confusion is the costliest error in the topic.
Adding when you should multiply. Successive independent choices multiply; mutually exclusive cases add. Writing 'OR = +, AND = ×' at the top of the sheet is not optional.
Forgetting repeated letters in word problems. MATHEMATICS has M×2, A×2, T×2, and missing any one of them makes the answer wrong by a clean factor of 2.
'At least one' computed as 'exactly one' — a systematic under-count that has a plausible-looking option waiting for it.
Circular arrangements computed as n! instead of (n−1)!.

Number-formation questions: 'how many 3-digit numbers' excludes those beginning with 0, and 'digits may repeat' versus 'cannot repeat' changes the entire method. Both conditions live in the stem and both must be read.
q-permutation.timeTarget: 50-70 seconds per question. A plain nCr selection should be under 40 seconds; a conditional committee problem may take up to 90.
q-permutation.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you can correctly state P or C within 5 seconds on 10 of 10 fresh question stems, compute any nCr with n ≤ 15 in under 20 seconds using the nC(n−r) shortcut, and reach for the complement automatically on every 'at least one' question rather than enumerating cases.

The same setup asked as both a counting question and a probability question in consecutive questions (Mains).
Handshakes, diagonals of a polygon, or round-robin matches — all nC2 in disguise.

q-probability.whatItIs: P(event) = favourable ÷ total, with the counting done by combinations. At Clerk level it is almost always a bag of coloured balls, a pack of cards, or dice.
q-probability.coreMethod:
1. Write the TOTAL first: total = nCr where n is all the items and r is how many are drawn. This is the denominator for the whole question — compute it once and box it.
2. Write the FAVOURABLE count using the same combination logic, respecting the stated condition.
3. Divide and reduce. Bank answers are always clean fractions.
4. 'At least one' → 1 − P(none). Never enumerate cases.
5. 'Either A or B' when mutually exclusive → add. 'A and B' when independent → multiply. If they are not mutually exclusive, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
6. Two-colour draws: from 5 red and 7 blue, P(both red on a draw of 2) = 5C2 ÷ 12C2 = 10/66 = 5/33.
7. Standard reference numbers on instant recall:
   • A pack of 52: 26 red, 26 black, 13 per suit, 4 aces, 12 face cards, 4 of each rank
   • Two dice: 36 outcomes; P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6; P(doubles) = 6/36 = 1/6
   • n coins → 2ⁿ outcomes
8. WITHOUT replacement the denominator shrinks with each draw, so multiply sequential probabilities. WITH replacement the denominator is constant.
tricks: Compute the denominator once and reuse it — bank probability questions usually arrive in linked pairs sharing the same bag.
'At least one' = 1 − P(none) turns a three-case sum into a single subtraction. This is the highest-value single habit in the topic.
Reduce before you multiply: take 10/66 to 5/33 before it enters any further computation.
'One ball of each colour' from three colours is a plain product (5 × 7 × 3), not a sum of combinations.
Card denominators are almost always 52C1 = 52, 52C2 = 1326 or 52C3 = 22100. Recognising 1326 saves computing 52×51/2 every time.
Sanity check against the options: if every option exceeds 1/2 and your answer is below 1/2, you have computed the complement. Flip it rather than restarting.
traps: With versus without replacement. The paper states it in a single word and it changes the denominator of every subsequent draw.
'At least two' computed as 'exactly two' — the same under-count trap as in permutation and combination.
'Two cards are drawn' defaults to WITHOUT replacement unless the stem says otherwise. Assuming replacement is a silent, systematic error.
Using permutations for the favourable count while using combinations for the total (or the reverse). The two must be counted the same way — the ordering convention must match top and bottom.
Adding probabilities of events that are NOT mutually exclusive without subtracting the overlap. 'A king or a heart' has an overlap of one card.
Careless fraction reduction: 10/66 reduces to 5/33, not to 1/6.6. Any non-integer denominator means you have made an error.
q-probability.timeTarget: 45-60 seconds per question. A bag-of-balls question with a single condition should land under 45 seconds.
q-probability.masteryCheck: You have mastered this when you compute the denominator BEFORE reading the condition, apply 1 − P(none) reflexively on every 'at least one' question, and clear 10 fresh bag-of-balls questions in under 8 minutes with 8 or more correct. Secondary check: you can state 52C2 = 1326 and P(sum of two dice = 7) = 1/6 without computing either.
questionPatterns: 'A bag contains 4 red, 5 green and 6 blue balls. Two are drawn at random. Find the probability that both are green / at least one is red / none is blue.'
'A card is drawn from a well-shuffled pack. What is the probability that it is a king or a heart?' — the overlap trap.
'Two dice are thrown. Find the probability that the sum is 8 / that the sum is a prime number.'
'Three coins are tossed. Find the probability of at least two heads.'
Probability appearing as one half of a Quantity I / Quantity II pair (Mains).
Probability derived from values in a DI table (Mains arithmetic DI).
Sequential draws without replacement, requiring a product of two changing fractions.

q-calc.topicName: Calculation toolkit + Simplification I (BODMAS, roots, indices)
q-calc.whatItIs: The raw arithmetic engine — tables, squares, cubes, fraction-percentage equivalents — plus single-expression simplification where you must produce the EXACT value of a BODMAS string containing fractions, decimals, roots and powers. It is not a maths topic; it is a reflex topic.
q-calc.coreMethod:
1. BUILD THE TOOLKIT (background drill, 10 min every day, runs in parallel with all other topics — do not try to finish it in one sitting):
   - Tables 2 to 30. Most people stop at 20; 21-30 is where the actual speed is, because DI and arithmetic constantly throw 24x, 27x, 18x at you.
   - Squares 1 to 40. Beyond 25, use structure instead of memory: (50+a)^2 = 2500 + 100a + a^2, so 57^2 = 2500+700+49 = 3249. (100-a)^2 = 10000 - 200a + a^2, so 96^2 = 10000-800+16 = 9216. For 30-50 use n^2 = (n+d)(n-d) + d^2, so 38^2 = 40x36 + 4 = 1444.
   - Any number ending in 5: n5^2 = [n x (n+1)] then '25'. 35^2 = 3x4|25 = 1225. 85^2 = 8x9|25 = 7225. 115^2 = 11x12|25 = 13225.
   - Cubes 1 to 20 (know 12^3=1728, 13^3=2197, 14^3=2744, 15^3=3375, 16^3=4096, 17^3=4913, 18^3=5832, 19^3=6859 cold — these ARE the cube-root questions).
   - Fraction-to-percentage table 1/2 to 1/20 AND the useful multiples: 1/2=50, 1/3=33.33, 2/3=66.67, 1/4=25, 3/4=75, 1/5=20, 2/5=40, 3/5=60, 1/6=16.67, 5/6=83.33, 1/7=14.28, 2/7=28.57, 3/7=42.86, 1/8=12.5, 3/8=37.5, 5/8=62.5, 7/8=87.5, 1/9=11.11, 2/9=22.22, 1/11=9.09, 1/12=8.33, 1/13=7.69, 1/14=7.14, 1/15=6.67, 1/16=6.25, 1/18=5.55, 1/20=5, 1/24=4.16, 1/40=2.5.
2. ORDER OF OPERATIONS as IBPS actually applies it: Brackets -> 'of' -> Division -> Multiplication -> Addition -> Subtraction. 'of' is multiplication but it binds BEFORE division. '1/2 of 60 / 3' = 30/3 = 10, not 1/2 x 20.
3. CONVERT DECIMALS TO FRACTIONS BEFORE MULTIPLYING. 0.125 = 1/8, 0.0625 = 1/16, 0.375 = 3/8, 0.625 = 5/8, 0.16(6) = 1/6, 0.833 = 5/6, 0.2857 = 2/7, 0.04 = 1/25. '0.0625 x 6400 / 0.4' becomes (1/16 x 6400) x (5/2) = 400 x 2.5 = 1000 in one line, versus three lines of decimal multiplication.
4. SQUARE ROOTS BY LAST DIGIT + BRACKET (5 seconds, no long division): the last digit of the number tells you the last digit of the root — 1->1 or 9, 4->2 or 8, 5->5, 6->4 or 6, 9->3 or 7, 0->0. Then bracket the magnitude between two known squares. sqrt(5184): ends in 4 so root ends 2 or 8; 4900 < 5184 < 6400 so root is 70-something; 5184 < 75^2 = 5625 so it is 72.
5. CUBE ROOTS BY LAST DIGIT + STRIP: last digit map (cube -> root) is 1->1, 8->2, 7->3, 4->4, 5->5, 6->6, 3->7, 2->8, 9->9, 0->0. Then strip the last three digits and bracket. cbrt(12167): ends in 7 -> root ends 3; strip to get 12, and 2^3=8 < 12 < 27=3^3, so tens digit is 2 -> answer 23.
6. INDICES: force everything to a single base before touching the exponents. (343)^? x 49 = 7^11 becomes 7^(3?) x 7^2 = 7^11 -> 3? + 2 = 11 -> ? = 3. Remember a^-n = 1/a^n and a^(1/2) = sqrt(a); IBPS uses negative fractional powers specifically to make you fumble the sign.
7. IDENTIFY WHAT '?' ACTUALLY IS before you start. If the expression is '?^2 = ...' the answer is the square root of what you compute. If it is 'sqrt(?) = ...' the answer is the square of what you compute. Circle the '?' form first — this is the single most common source of a wrong-but-confident answer.
tricks: Multiply by 25 as x100/4, by 125 as x1000/8, by 5 as x10/2, by 15 as x30/2, by 35 as x70/2, by 45 as x90/2, by 75 as x300/4. '384 x 25' is 38400/4 = 9600 in one step.
Percentage of a number always via the fraction table, never via decimals. 37.5% of 96 = 3/8 x 96 = 36. 62.5% of 128 = 5/8 x 128 = 80. 16.67% of 342 = 342/6 = 57. This is 3-4x faster than 96 x 0.375.
Nikhilam base method for two numbers near 100: 96 x 93 -> deficits 4 and 7 -> (96-7)|(4x7) = 89|28 = 8928. Same for numbers near 50 (halve the left part) and near 1000.
a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b) on sight. 87^2 - 13^2 = 100 x 74 = 7400. IBPS plants this in simplification strings constantly and it converts a two-square calculation into one multiplication.

Cancel across the whole expression before computing anything. In a chain of x and /, hunt for the pair that cancels (a 144 upstairs and a 12 downstairs) and kill it first — do not evaluate left to right.
Add and subtract left-to-right in your head using round anchors: 4879 + 2346 = 4879 + 2000 + 300 + 46 = 7225. Never stack columns on paper for 4-digit sums.
traps: Solving for the wrong thing: the answer options contain BOTH 144 and 12 when the question is '?^2 = ...'. You compute 144 correctly and lose the mark. Always read the '?' form twice.

'of' vs '/' ordering. '2/5 of 350 / 7' = 140/7 = 20. Treating 'of' as ordinary multiplication after division gives 2/5 x 50 = 20 here by luck, but in '1/3 of 90 / 5 x 2' the two readings diverge — do 'of' first, always.
Decimal place shift on multiplication of two decimals: 0.05 x 0.05 = 0.0025, not 0.025. IBPS puts both in the options.
A minus sign before a bracket. '250 - (60 - 15 x 3)' = 250 - (60-45) = 235, not 250 - 60 + 45. People distribute the minus without finishing inside the bracket first.

Assuming a root is exact. sqrt(1225) = 35 exactly, but sqrt(1250) is not an integer — if your last-digit method gives no clean candidate, the question is an approximation question, not a simplification one.
q-calc.timeTarget: 15-20 seconds per question (10-12 seconds for a pure BODMAS chain with clean fractions; up to 25 seconds for a multi-radical or indices question). If you are past 30 seconds you have misread something — restart or leave.
q-calc.masteryCheck: You can recite tables 12-30, squares 1-40 and cubes 1-20 aloud with no pause in under 6 minutes total; you produce sqrt(5184), sqrt(6561), cbrt(12167) and cbrt(5832) in under 5 seconds each with no written working; and you score 15/15 on a fresh 15-question BODMAS simplification set in 4 minutes flat.
questionPatterns: Pure BODMAS with mixed numbers: (4 5/7 / 2 1/3) x 1 2/5 + 3 = ?
Radical chain: sqrt(1296) + sqrt(2401) - sqrt(784) = ?
