q-simpl-2.whatItIs: Questions that say 'what APPROXIMATE value will come in place of the question mark' — every number is deliberately messy (19.98, 1439.85, 624.99) and the options are spaced far enough apart that rounding is safe. It tests whether you have the nerve to stop calculating.
q-simpl-2.coreMethod:
1. READ THE OPTIONS FIRST — before you look at the expression. The gap between options tells you how hard you are allowed to round. If options are 180/195/210/225/240 (7-8% apart) you can round aggressively. If they are 193/195/197/199/201 you must stay within 1% and round only the obviously-near-integer terms.
2. ROUND EVERY TERM TO ITS NEAREST FRIENDLY ANCHOR: 19.98 -> 20, 24.97 -> 25, 33.29 -> 33.33 (= 1/3), 12.49 -> 12.5 (= 1/8), 624.99 -> 625, 1439.85 -> 1440, 4879 -> 4880 or 4900 depending on option spacing.
3. TRACK THE DIRECTION OF YOUR ERROR. Write a small + or - next to each rounding. If you rounded the numerator UP and the denominator DOWN, your result is too big — when two options straddle your value, take the lower one. This single habit converts most 'my answer is between two options' moments into a correct pick.
4. ROOTS: sqrt(624.99) is sqrt(625) = 25. sqrt(3480) -> nearest perfect square 3481 = 59^2 -> 59. cbrt(1330) -> 1331 = 11^3 -> 11. cbrt(4090) -> 4096 = 16^3 -> 16. Build the habit of scanning your squares-to-40 and cubes-to-20 list for the nearest neighbour.
5. NON-NEIGHBOUR ROOTS: sqrt(N) where N is not near a perfect square — use sqrt(a^2 + d) = a + d/(2a). sqrt(1700) = sqrt(1681 + 19) = 41 + 19/82 = 41.23.
6. PERCENTAGES VIA THE FRACTION TABLE: 39.98% of 449.9 = 2/5 x 450 = 180. 16.68% of 1199 = 1200/6 = 200. 14.29% of 699 = 700/7 = 100. Never multiply by 0.3998.
7. SPOT a^2 - b^2: (17.95)^2 - (12.02)^2 -> (18-12)(18+12) = 180. Two squarings become one multiplication.
8. '?%' QUESTIONS: '?% of 559.87 + 45.02% of 799.99 = 419.99' -> ?% of 560 + 360 = 420 -> ?% of 560 = 60 -> ? = 60/560 x 100 = 10.7 -> pick the nearest option (11 or 10).
9. STOP THE MOMENT ONE OPTION IS CLEARLY CLOSEST. Do not compute the second decimal place to feel safe.
tricks: Options-first is the whole technique. Two options 5%+ apart means you may round to the nearest 10 or even 50 and still be safe — that turns a 40-second question into a 12-second one.
Signed rounding log: put + or - beside each rounded term. Net + means your answer is an overestimate. Costs one second, resolves the straddle.

Convert every messy percentage to the nearest table fraction: 12.51%->1/8, 16.65%->1/6, 20.03%->1/5, 24.98%->1/4, 33.31%->1/3, 14.27%->1/7, 11.09%->1/9. The whole approximation paper is built out of these.
Squares and cubes as anchors: memorising squares to 40 and cubes to 20 means you almost never have to actually extract a root in an approximation question — you just recognise the neighbour.
When a term like 8.97 x 41.03 appears, do 9 x 41 = 369, then note both roundings went opposite ways so the error nearly cancels — no correction needed. Opposite-direction roundings are free accuracy.
x% of y = y% of x. '48% of 250' = '250% of 48' = 120. Useful when one of the two numbers is the friendlier one.
traps: Options planted close together specifically to punish lazy rounding — e.g. 195 and 185 both present when the true value is 189.6. Always check option spacing BEFORE deciding how hard to round.
Rounding a small decimal that gets multiplied by a large number: turning 0.48 into 0.5 inside '0.48 x 2000' shifts the answer by 40. Round the small multiplier LAST and least.
Compounding same-direction errors: rounding 19.8 up to 20 AND 49.7 up to 50 in a product inflates the result by ~1.4%. If options are 2% apart that is fatal.
Treating a cube as a square. (12.03)^3 is 1728-ish, not 144-ish; and a 1% error in the base becomes a 3% error in the cube.
Wasting time exact-solving because one option happens to match exactly. If the question word is 'approximate', the setter has given you permission to be sloppy — take it.

q-numsys.whatItIs: Divisibility, unit digits, remainders, and the HCF/LCM word problems (bells tolling together, greatest number that divides leaving remainders, least number leaving a common remainder). Low direct weight, but the LCM habit powers Time-and-Work and Pipes.
q-numsys.coreMethod:
1. HCF by Euclid's division: divide the larger by the smaller, then the divisor by the remainder, repeat until remainder 0. HCF(1001, 910): 1001 = 910x1 + 91; 910 = 91x10 + 0 -> HCF = 91.
2. LCM by prime powers: take the highest power of each prime present. LCM(12,18,20) = 2^2 x 3^2 x 5 = 180. For two numbers only, LCM = product / HCF.
3. MASTER IDENTITY: Product of two numbers = HCF x LCM. Also, the two numbers are ALWAYS H x a and H x b where H is the HCF and a, b are coprime. 'HCF is 12, LCM is 144, one number is 36 — find the other': other = 12x144/36 = 48.
4. THE FIVE WORD-PROBLEM FORMS (learn these as templates, they are the whole topic):
   a. Greatest number that divides x, y, z leaving remainders a, b, c -> HCF(x-a, y-b, z-c).
   b. Greatest number that divides x, y, z leaving the SAME (unknown) remainder -> HCF of the pairwise differences: HCF(y-x, z-y, z-x).
   c. Least number which when divided by a, b, c leaves the same remainder r -> LCM(a,b,c) + r.
   d. Least number which when divided by a, b, c leaves remainders p, q, r where (a-p) = (b-q) = (c-r) = k -> LCM(a,b,c) - k.
   e. Bells/lights/traffic signals ringing together -> LCM of the intervals. Number of times in T seconds INCLUDING the start = T/LCM + 1.
5. FRACTIONS: HCF of fractions = HCF(numerators)/LCM(denominators). LCM of fractions = LCM(numerators)/HCF(denominators).
6. UNIT DIGIT via cyclicity 4: divide the power by 4, use the remainder; remainder 0 means use the 4th term. Cycles: 2 -> (2,4,8,6); 3 -> (3,9,7,1); 7 -> (7,9,3,1); 8 -> (8,4,2,6); 4 -> (4,6); 9 -> (9,1); 0,1,5,6 -> themselves. Unit digit of 7^83: 83 = 4x20+3 -> third term of (7,9,3,1) -> 3.
7. DIVISIBILITY RULES worth knowing: by 4 (last two digits), 8 (last three), 3 and 9 (digit sum), 11 (alternating digit sum divisible by 11), 7 (double the last digit and subtract from the rest, repeat), 6 (2 and 3 together).
8. REMAINDER SHORTCUT: to find the remainder of a product, take remainders first and multiply them. Remainder of (17 x 23) / 5 = (2 x 3)/5 -> 6/5 -> 1.
tricks: Product = HCF x LCM turns almost every two-number question into one division. Also use it to sanity-check: HCF must divide LCM exactly — if it doesn't, you've misread the question.
For 'same remainder, remainder unknown', go straight to the DIFFERENCES. Beginners waste 60 seconds trying to guess the remainder.

Bells: the answer to 'how many times in 1 hour' is 3600/LCM + 1, and the +1 (the initial simultaneous ring) is what the options are testing. Also check whether the LCM is in seconds while the period is in minutes.
Build LCMs of small numbers by prime powers, not by long division ladders — LCM(8,12,15,20) = 2^3 x 3 x 5 = 120 takes four seconds.
Unit digit of any number ending in 5 or 6 raised to any power is 5 or 6. Numbers ending in 0 give 0, in 1 give 1. That kills half the unit-digit questions instantly.
traps: Confusing template (a) with template (b): 'leaving remainders 3, 5, 7' is a different calculation from 'leaving the same remainder'.
Off-by-one on the bells problem — forgetting that they also rang together at the start.
Intervals given in seconds but the question asks 'in 2 hours' — convert before, not after.
Remainder larger than the divisor in your working, or an option where the remainder exceeds the divisor — that option is always wrong, eliminate it free.
HCF/LCM of fractions: swapping the two formulas. HCF uses HCF on top; LCM uses LCM on top. Say it aloud: 'the operation name goes on top'.

q-percentage.whatItIs: The spine of the entire Quant section. Profit-loss, interest, DI, mixture and data comparison are all percentage questions in costume. It tests whether you can move between a percentage, a fraction and a ratio without computing.
q-percentage.coreMethod:
1. NEVER MULTIPLY BY A DECIMAL. Convert to the table fraction and cancel. 62.5% of 288 = 5/8 x 288 = 180. 8.33% of 1560 = 1560/12 = 130.
2. 'A IS x% MORE/LESS THAN B' -> convert to a RATIO immediately. x% more, where x = 1/n as a fraction, gives A:B = (n+1):n. So: 25% (1/4) more -> 5:4. 20% (1/5) more -> 6:5. 33.33% (1/3) more -> 4:3. 16.67% (1/6) more -> 7:6. 12.5% (1/8) more -> 9:8. 11.11% (1/9) more -> 10:9. For 'less', flip: 20% less -> 4:5; 25% less -> 3:4.
3. THE REVERSE PAIR (memorise as pairs, this is the highest-yield single fact in the topic): if A is 1/n MORE than B, then B is 1/(n+1) LESS than A. So 25% more <-> 20% less; 33.33% more <-> 25% less; 20% more <-> 16.67% less; 12.5% more <-> 11.11% less; 100% more <-> 50% less. IBPS asks this both ways every year.
4. SUCCESSIVE CHANGE: net% = a + b + ab/100, signs included. +20% then -10% -> 20 - 10 - 200/100 = +8%. Or just multiply the fractions: 6/5 x 9/10 = 54/50 = +8%.
5. EQUAL UP-THEN-DOWN is always a LOSS of x^2/100 %. +20% then -20% -> 4% net loss. Never zero.
6. UNITARY, NOT ALGEBRA: 'if 15% of a number is 45, what is 40% of it?' -> 45/15 x 40 = 120. Do not find the number.
7. THE MARKS PATTERN: 'A scores 30% and fails by 40 marks; B scores 45% and gets 20 marks more than the pass mark.' The DIFFERENCE in percentages maps to the DIFFERENCE in marks: 15% = 60 marks -> total = 400. Pass mark = 120+40 = 160.
8. EXPENDITURE / CONSUMPTION: if price rises by x%, consumption must fall by x/(100+x) x 100 % to keep expenditure constant. Price up 25% (1/4) -> consumption down 1/5 = 20%. This is just the reverse-pair rule again.
9. TWO-STEP POPULATION/SALARY: P x (1 + a/100) x (1 - b/100). Use fraction multipliers (11/10, 6/5, 9/10, 4/5) so the numbers cancel against P.
10. ALWAYS UNDERLINE THE BASE. Write '% of WHAT' beside every percentage in the question before you compute anything.
tricks: The reverse-pair table (25% more = 20% less, 33.33% more = 25% less, 20% more = 16.67% less, 12.5% more = 11.11% less, 16.67% more = 14.28% less) converts a whole class of questions into a 3-second lookup.
x% of y = y% of x. 18% of 50 = 50% of 18 = 9. 64% of 25 = 25% of 64 = 16. Use whichever side is friendlier.
To increase by a table fraction, multiply directly: +37.5% is x11/8; +62.5% is x13/8; +12.5% is x9/8; +16.67% is x7/6. To decrease: -37.5% is x5/8; -16.67% is x5/6.
Equal-percentage up-then-down is ALWAYS x^2/100 loss. If an option says 'no change', it is wrong by construction.
In marks/pass-fail problems, subtract the two scenarios first — the unknown total drops out of a difference and you get the total in one division.
15% = 10% + 5% (halve the ten); 45% = 50% - 5%; 35% = 25% + 10%. Building percentages out of 10%, 5% and 1% chunks beats any multiplication.
traps: Percentage POINTS vs percent. A rise from 20% to 25% is 5 percentage points but a 25% increase. IBPS puts both 5 and 25 in the options.
Adding successive percentages: 20% then 20% is 44%, not 40%; 20% then -20% is -4%, not 0.
Base shifting mid-question: 'B is 20% less than A' does NOT mean 'A is 20% more than B'. It means A is 25% more than B.
'x% more than' vs 'x% of'. '60% more than 200' is 320; '60% of 200' is 120. Both appear as options.
In pass-fail problems, confusing the TOTAL marks with the PASSING marks — the question usually asks for one and the fast route gives you the other first.

q-ratio.whatItIs: Splitting quantities in a given ratio, combining chained ratios, and handling ratios that change when a fixed amount is added or removed. It is the second spine after percentage, and it is the language every partnership, mixture and age question is written in.
q-ratio.coreMethod:
1. ONE VARIABLE ONLY. a:b = 3:5 becomes 3k and 5k. Never introduce two letters — every ratio question is a single linear equation in k.
2. DIFFERENCE-OF-PARTS is the fastest tool. If a:b = 5:8 and b - a = 24, then 3 parts = 24, so k = 8, giving 40 and 64. Similarly sum-of-parts: if a:b = 5:8 and a + b = 91, then 13 parts = 91, k = 7.
3. CHAINING TWO RATIOS: A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5. Make B common by cross-multiplying: A:B:C = (2x4):(3x4):(3x5) = 8:12:15. Rule: multiply the first ratio by the second's B-term, and the second ratio by the first's B-term.
4. CHAINING THREE: A:B = 2:3, B:C = 4:5, C:D = 6:7 -> A:B:C:D = (2x4x6):(3x4x6):(3x5x6):(3x5x7) = 48:72:90:105 -> divide by 3 -> 16:24:30:35.
5. RATIO CHANGES ON ADDING n: 'the ratio of two numbers is 3:5; if 4 is added to each it becomes 5:7' -> (3k+4)/(5k+4) = 5/7 -> 21k+28 = 25k+20 -> k = 2.
6. FRACTIONAL RELATIONS -> RATIO: 'A gets two-thirds of what B gets, B gets one-quarter of what C gets.' Set C = 1, B = 1/4, A = 2/3 x 1/4 = 1/6. Multiply through by 12: A:B:C = 2:3:12.
7. PROPORTION VOCABULARY (each is one formula, learn all four): a:b :: c:d means ad = bc. Mean proportional between a and b = sqrt(ab). Third proportional to a and b = b^2/a. Fourth proportional to a, b, c = bc/a.
8. DIVIDING A SUM: each share = (own parts / total parts) x total sum. To get the DIFFERENCE of two shares directly: (difference of parts / total parts) x sum — do not compute both shares.
9. INVERSE RATIO: 'divided in inverse ratio 2:3' means divided in 3:2. Also 'in the ratio of the reciprocals 1/2 : 1/3' = 3:2.
10. BACK-SUBSTITUTE FROM OPTIONS when the options are the actual quantities — checking one option against the stated condition takes 10 seconds and often beats solving forward.
tricks: Difference-of-parts / sum-of-parts: whenever the question gives you 'their difference is D' or 'their sum is S', you get k in one division. This alone covers a third of ratio questions.

Adding the SAME number to both terms always moves the ratio TOWARDS 1:1; subtracting moves it AWAY. Use this to sanity-check your k before finishing — if your answer moves the ratio the wrong way, you made a sign error.
Ratio to percentage via the fraction table: in 3:5 the first is 3/8 = 37.5% of the total and the second is 62.5%. Instant, no division.

Chaining: instead of the cross-multiply rule, just scale to the LCM of the shared term. A:B = 2:3, B:C = 4:5 -> LCM of the two B-values (3 and 4) is 12 -> A:B = 8:12, B:C = 12:15 -> 8:12:15. Fewer multiplications, less to write.
Difference of two shares = (parts difference / total parts) x sum — one calculation instead of two.
When three or more quantities are in a chain of fractional relations, set the LAST one to 1, work backwards, then clear denominators with the LCM. Faster than any simultaneous setup.
traps: Order reversal: 'the ratio of B to A' when you computed A to B. IBPS always puts the reversed value in the options.
Adding ratios directly: 2:3 combined with 3:4 is not 5:7. There is no addition of ratios.

When the same quantity appears in two ratios with different numbers (B is 3 in one and 4 in the other), you must scale to the LCM first. Reading it as 3 = 4 is the single most common wreck in this topic.
Ratio given for PAST or FUTURE values but the question asks for the PRESENT value.
Applying a percentage change to 'k' instead of to the actual quantity, so the answer comes out a factor of k off.

q-average.whatItIs: Recovering a total from a mean and vice versa, and handling what happens to the mean when a member joins, leaves or is replaced. Almost every question reduces to one line: change in total = n x change in average.
q-average.coreMethod:
1. Average = Sum / n. Every question is really 'recover the SUM'.
2. THE MASTER LINE: change in total = n x change in average. Use it for all three variants:
   - Someone JOINS: 'average of 10 people is 32; a new person joins and the average becomes 33' -> total rose by 10x1 = 10 above the new average, so the new person = 33 + 10 = 43. (Equivalently: new member = new average + n x change.)
   - Someone is REPLACED: 'average of 10 rises by 2 when a person of weight 25 is replaced' -> new person = 25 + 10x2 = 45.
   - Someone LEAVES: 'average of 12 is 40; one leaves and the average of the rest is 39' -> the leaver = 40 + 11x1 = 51.
3. DEVIATION METHOD for averaging a raw list: pick a convenient anchor, average the deviations, add back. For 46, 52, 48, 54, 50 anchor at 50 -> deviations -4, +2, -2, +4, 0 -> mean deviation 0 -> average 50. Never add five three-digit numbers.
4. CONSECUTIVE / EVENLY SPACED: average = (first + last)/2 = the middle term. Average of 11 consecutive integers whose sum is 253 -> average 23 -> that IS the middle term.
5. STANDARD SUMS: first n natural numbers average = (n+1)/2; first n odd numbers average = n; first n even numbers average = n+1; sum of first n naturals = n(n+1)/2.
6. WEIGHTED AVERAGE: (n1a1 + n2a2)/(n1+n2). To go BACKWARDS from a combined average to the group ratio, use alligation — it is faster than algebra.
7. AVERAGE SPEED: for equal DISTANCES use the harmonic mean 2xy/(x+y); for three equal distances 3xyz/(xy+yz+zx). For equal TIMES use the plain mean (x+y)/2. Decide which by reading whether the question says 'half the distance' or 'half the time'.
8. AGE-AVERAGE OVER TIME: the total age of a group of n people grows by n every year. 'The average age of a family of 5 was 25 five years ago; a baby was born — the average is still 25 today.' Total then = 125; five years on the same 5 people total 150; now 6 people average 25 means total 150 — so the baby is 0? Recompute carefully: 150 + baby = 6 x 25 = 150 -> baby's age 0. Always set up the two totals explicitly rather than reasoning verbally.
9. EXCLUDING EXTREMES: 'average excluding the highest and lowest' -> subtract those two values from the total and divide by n-2.
tricks: 'n x change in average' is one line and solves the join/leave/replace family — which is most of the topic. Write it on your card and use nothing else for those.
Deviation method removes all multi-digit addition. Anchor on the value nearest the middle of the list.
For consecutive or evenly spaced numbers, the average IS the middle term — no addition at all. If there is an even count, it is the mean of the two middle terms.
Cricket-innings pattern: new average = old average + (new score - old average)/(n+1). 'Average after 16 innings is 36, scores 87 in the 17th' -> 36 + 51/17 = 39.
When two groups combine, use alligation to find the group sizes from the three averages — it converts a two-equation problem into a subtraction.
Sanity-check direction: the combined average must always lie between the two group averages. If yours doesn't, you swapped a weight.
traps: Average speed for equal distances computed as the simple mean. 60 and 40 km/h over equal distances gives 48, not 50 — and 50 is always in the options.
Getting n wrong by one: does the new average cover n or n+1 people? Write the count beside each average before starting.
'The average increased by 2' vs 'the average became 2' — misreading this inverts the whole question.
Averaging two averages of different-sized groups as if the groups were equal.
Forcing an integer answer. Ages and scores frequently average to a fraction; an option like 39.5 is often correct.

q-ages.whatItIs: Two or three people whose ages are given as a ratio now and a different ratio at some other time. It is a one-variable linear equation dressed up in tense changes, and it appears in almost every Clerk Prelims paper.
q-ages.coreMethod:
1. SET AGES AS RATIO PARTS, not letters. Ratio 4:5 now -> present ages are 4x and 5x. Only use separate letters if no ratio is given.
2. APPLY THE TENSE SHIFT TO EVERY PERSON. 'Five years ago' subtracts 5 from ALL of them; 'after 8 years' adds 8 to ALL of them. Write the shifted ages in a second row underneath before forming the equation.
3. FORM ONE EQUATION AND CROSS-MULTIPLY. Present 3:4, after 6 years 5:6 -> (3x+6)/(4x+6) = 5/6 -> 18x + 36 = 20x + 30 -> x = 3 -> ages 9 and 12.
4. THE DIRECT FORMULA (worth memorising — it turns the whole question into one line). If the present ratio is a:b and at time t the ratio is c:d, then x = t(c - d) / (ad - bc), where t is POSITIVE for 'after t years' and NEGATIVE for 't years ago'. Check: present 3:4, after 6 years 5:6 -> x = 6(5-6)/(3x6 - 4x5) = -6/-2 = 3. Correct. Present 4:5, after 5 years 5:6 -> x = 5(5-6)/(4x6 - 5x5) = -5/-1 = 5 -> ages 20 and 25. Correct.
5. THE DIFFERENCE OF TWO AGES IS CONSTANT FOREVER. This is the master lever. If A is 6 years older than B today, A - B = 6 at every point in the past and future. Use it whenever the question mixes a ratio with an absolute gap: 'ages are 5x and 8x and the difference is 12' -> 3x = 12 -> x = 4.
6. SUM-AND-CONDITION TYPE: 'the sum of present ages of father and son is 60; six years ago the father was five times the son.' F + S = 60 and F - 6 = 5(S - 6). Substitute F = 60 - S: 54 - S = 5S - 30 -> 6S = 84 -> S = 14, F = 46.
7. THREE-PERSON: identify which two are in the ratio and which one is tied by an absolute statement. Solve the ratio pair first, then plug in.
8. BACK-SUBSTITUTE FROM OPTIONS when the options are ages. Testing one option against the stated past/future condition takes 10 seconds and often beats forming the equation.
9. FINALLY, RE-READ WHAT IS ASKED: present age, age after n years, the sum, the difference, or the ratio. The options always contain more than one of these.
tricks: The direct formula x = t(c-d)/(ad-bc) with signed t answers the standard two-ratio question in one line — roughly 25 seconds saved over setting up and expanding a cross-multiplication.
Constant difference: divide the absolute age gap by the difference of the ratio parts to get one part instantly. Ratio 5:8 with a gap of 12 -> one part = 4.
When BOTH 'n years ago' and 'n years hence' appear, subtract the two equations — the constants cancel and you are left with a single term.
Option back-substitution is legitimately fast here because verifying is a subtraction and a multiplication. Try the middle option first and use the direction of the miss to jump to the right one.
If the two ratios move in the 'wrong' direction (the ratio should always drift towards 1:1 as time passes forward), you have misread which ratio is present and which is past. Free error check.
traps: Applying the time shift to only one person. Always write the shifted row for everyone before forming the equation.
The ratio given is for PAST ages while the question asks for PRESENT ages — or vice versa. Underline the tense in both the given and the asked.
'A is twice as old as B' means A = 2B. 'A is older than B by twice B's age' means A = 3B. IBPS uses both phrasings.
Answering the present age when the question asks for the age after 5 years, or asking for the sum when you computed one age. Both values are in the options.
In three-person problems, assuming the third person is part of the ratio when the question only ties them by an absolute statement.
q-ages.timeTarget: 45-60 seconds per question. With the direct formula, a standard two-ratio question should take 30-35 seconds; a sum-plus-condition type 60.

q-pld-1.topicName: Profit, Loss & Discount I — CP, SP and percentage basics
q-pld-1.whatItIs: The arithmetic of buying and selling. Cost Price (CP) is what the seller paid, Selling Price (SP) is what the buyer paid. Profit = SP − CP, Loss = CP − SP, and in every IBPS question the percentage is calculated ON THE COST PRICE unless the question says otherwise in so many words. The single relation that generates everything is SP = CP × (100 + P%)/100, where P% is negative for a loss. This first half covers the direct forms: find any one of CP / SP / profit%, the 'if he had sold for Rs.X more' family, the two-articles-same-SP family, the 'CP of a articles = SP of b articles' family, and the dishonest-dealer false-weight family. Marked price and discount chains are the second half (q-pld-2). Questions appear as standalone word problems in Prelims and inside the Mains arithmetic mix and occasionally as a Data Sufficiency pair.
q-pld-1.coreMethod:
THE MULTIPLIER ENGINE — 4 steps, use it for every question:
1. Convert the percentage to a FRACTION from the memorised table, not a decimal. 25%=1/4, 20%=1/5, 16⅔%=1/6, 14²/₇%=1/7, 12½%=1/8, 11⅑%=1/9, 10%=1/10, 9¹/₁₁%=1/11, 8⅓%=1/12, 6¼%=1/16.
2. Turn it into a CP : SP ratio. A profit of 1/n means CP : SP = n : n+1. A loss of 1/n means CP : SP = n : n−1. So 25% profit is CP:SP = 4:5; 20% loss is CP:SP = 5:4.
3. Multiply or divide in that ratio. Going CP→SP multiply by SP/CP; going SP→CP multiply by CP/SP. There is no dividing by 100 anywhere.
4. If the question is purely percentages with no rupee figure, set CP = 100 (or CP = the LCM of the denominators involved) and read the answer straight off.

WORKED EXAMPLES (each one computed and checked):

A. Direct. An article is sold for Rs.1,120 at a profit of 12%. Find CP.
12% profit → CP:SP = 100:112 = 25:28. CP = 1120 × 25/28 = 1,000. Check: 1000 + 12% = 1,120. ✓

B. The 'Rs.X more' family. A man sells an article at a 20% loss. Had he sold it for Rs.140 more he would have gained 15%. Find CP.
Both percentages sit on the SAME base (CP), so the gap between the two selling prices is 20% + 15% = 35% of CP. 35% of CP = 140 → CP = 400. Check: 20% loss SP = 320; 320 + 140 = 460 = 400 × 1.15. ✓

C. Two articles, same SP. Two articles are sold at Rs.960 each, one at 20% profit and one at 20% loss. Overall result?
CP1 = 960 × 5/6 = 800. CP2 = 960 × 5/4 = 1,200. Total CP = 2,000, total SP = 1,920 → loss Rs.80 → 4% loss. Confirms the standard result: equal SP at ±x% is ALWAYS a loss of x²/100 % = 400/100 = 4%. ✓

D. Articles-equated family. The profit on selling 15 articles equals the selling price of 3 articles. Find profit%.
SP(15) − CP(15) = SP(3) → SP(12) = CP(15) → SP/CP = 15/12 = 5/4 → profit 25%. ✓

E. Buy-and-sell-in-lots. A man buys 12 oranges for Rs.10 and sells 10 oranges for Rs.12. Find profit%.
CP per orange = 10/12 = 5/6. SP per orange = 12/10 = 6/5. SP/CP = (6/5) ÷ (5/6) = 36/25 → profit = 11/25 = 44%. ✓

F. False weight. A dealer sells at cost price but uses a 900 g weight for 1 kg. Find gain%.
Gain% = error / (true weight − error) × 100 = 100/900 × 100 = 11⅑%. Check with the multiplier engine: he pays for 900 g, charges for 1000 g, so CP:SP = 900:1000 = 9:10, which is a 1/9 gain = 11⅑%. ✓
tricks: Fraction-first, always. 12½% of 4,800 via 1/8 is one division (600); via 0.125 it is a three-digit multiplication. Over 12 arithmetic questions this alone returns two to three minutes in a 20-minute sectional clock.

The articles-equated shortcut: if CP of a articles = SP of b articles, then profit% = (a − b)/b × 100. Check against worked example D — CP of 15 = SP of 12 gives (15−12)/12 = 25%, matching the long method. It turns a 45-second question into a 12-second one.

Equal-SP theorem: two articles sold at the SAME selling price, one at +x% and one at −x%, always produce a net LOSS of x²/100 percent. It is a proved identity, not a tendency — at ±10% the loss is 1%, at ±20% it is 4%, at ±25% it is 6.25%.

In 'sold for Rs.X more/less' problems, add the two percentages ONLY after confirming both are on CP — then the rupee gap divided by the summed percentage gives CP in one step. Worked example B is a 15-second question this way.

False-weight formula: gain% = error/(true value − error) × 100. Using 800 g for a kilo gives 200/800 = 25%; using 1,200 g when buying gives 200/1,200 = 16⅔%. Memorise the two directions (short-weighing when selling, over-taking when buying) rather than re-deriving under the clock.
When only percentages appear and no rupee figure, put CP = 100 and stop worrying about elegance — the answer will be a percentage anyway and the arithmetic becomes mental.
traps: Computing the percentage on SP instead of CP. If CP = 400 and SP = 500, the profit is 25% (100/400), not 20% (100/500). Both numbers will sit in the five options waiting for you.

Adding percentages that sit on different bases. In worked example B, 20 + 15 = 35 works because both are on CP. If one figure were 'a 15% gain on selling price', the addition is invalid and you must convert to a common base first.

Answering 'no profit no loss' on the equal-SP ±x% question. The +x% article has a smaller CP than the −x% article, so the loss on the bigger cost outweighs the gain on the smaller one. It is always a loss.

Confusing 'profit on selling 15 articles equals the SP of 3 articles' with 'profit on 15 articles equals the CP of 3 articles'. The first gives 25%, the second gives SP(15) = CP(18) → 20%. One word changes the answer.
In lot problems ('12 for Rs.10, sells 10 for Rs.12'), inverting one of the two rates. Write both as rupees-per-unit in the same direction before dividing, or the 44% becomes 20%.

Treating a false-weight gain as equal to the percentage error. Selling with a 900 g weight is an 11⅑% gain, not a 10% gain — the denominator is what he actually gave, 900, not the 1,000 he charged for.

q-pld-2.topicName: Profit, Loss & Discount II — successive discount, marked price and cost price
q-pld-2.whatItIs: The second half of the trading chain, where a third price enters. Marked Price (MP, also called list price, printed price or labelled price) is the tag on the item. Discount is always taken OFF THE MARKED PRICE. Profit is always measured AGAINST THE COST PRICE. The whole topic is one chain read left to right: CP → (mark up) → MP → (discount) → SP, and every question hands you two links and asks for the third. Successive discounts are simply two or more multipliers applied one after another to MP. The examiner's whole design here rests on the two different bases — a candidate who applies a discount to CP, or a markup to MP, produces a number that is sitting in the option list.
q-pld-2.coreMethod:
THE CHAIN METHOD — 5 steps:
1. Draw the chain on your rough sheet: CP → MP → SP. Three boxes.
2. Write the master relation: MP × (1 − d₁/100) × (1 − d₂/100) = SP = CP × (1 + p/100). Discounts multiply on the left of SP, profit multiplies on the right.
3. Convert every percentage to a fraction multiplier and cancel: 10% off = ×9/10, 12½% off = ×7/8, 15% off = ×17/20, 20% off = ×4/5, 25% off = ×3/4, 33⅓% off = ×2/3, 40% off = ×3/5. A 25% markup = ×5/4, 40% markup = ×7/5, 50% markup = ×3/2.
4. If no rupee figure is given, set CP = 100 when the question asks for profit%, and set MP = 100 when the question asks only about discounts. Never set both.
5. Read the answer off the chain. If the question asks for the EQUIVALENT SINGLE DISCOUNT, remember it is 100 minus the surviving percentage, not the surviving percentage itself.

SUCCESSIVE-DISCOUNT SHORTCUT: two discounts of a% and b% are equivalent to a single discount of (a + b − ab/100)%. For 20% and 10%: 30 − 2 = 28%. For 25% and 20%: 45 − 5 = 40%. For 10% and 10%: 20 − 1 = 19%.

THE BRIDGE FORMULA (the most useful line in the topic):
MP/CP = (100 + profit%) / (100 − discount%)
Given any two of markup, profit and discount, the third falls out in one step.

WORKED EXAMPLES (all computed and verified):

A. Straight chain. MP = Rs.2,000, successive discounts of 25% and 20%. Find SP and the equivalent single discount.
SP = 2000 × 3/4 × 4/5 = 1,200. Equivalent single discount = (2000 − 1200)/2000 = 40%. Shortcut check: 25 + 20 − (25×20)/100 = 45 − 5 = 40%. ✓

B. Markup then discount → profit. A shopkeeper marks his goods 40% above cost and allows a 25% discount. Find profit%.
CP = 100 → MP = 140 → SP = 140 × 3/4 = 105 → profit 5%. Bridge check: MP/CP = 140/100 = 1.4 and (100+5)/(100−25) = 105/75 = 1.4. ✓

C. Reverse direction. A trader wants a 20% profit after allowing a 20% discount. By what percent above cost must he mark the goods?
CP = 100 → SP must be 120 → MP = 120 ÷ 4/5 = 150 → mark up 50%. Bridge check: 120/80 = 150/100. ✓ Note that 20% up and 20% down do NOT cancel.

D. Find the missing discount. On an article marked Rs.800, two successive discounts of 20% and x% give a selling price of Rs.544. Find x.
800 × 4/5 = 640. 544/640 = 17/20 = 0.85, so the second multiplier is 85% → x = 15%. ✓

E. Discount and profit together. After allowing a 10% discount an article still yields an 8% profit. If CP is Rs.500, find MP.
SP = 500 × 27/25 = 540. MP = 540 ÷ 9/10 = 600. ✓ Bridge check: MP/CP = 600/500 = 1.2 and 108/90 = 1.2. ✓

F. Three multipliers. MP = Rs.1,600 with discounts of 25%, 20% and a further 10% cash discount on the reduced amount.
1600 × 3/4 × 4/5 × 9/10 = 864. Equivalent single discount = (1600 − 864)/1600 = 46%. Note it is NOT 25 + 20 + 10 = 55%. ✓
tricks: The bridge formula MP/CP = (100 + profit%)/(100 − discount%) answers the three commonest question types in one line each. In worked example C it replaces a three-step chain with a single division, saving roughly 25 seconds per question.

Successive discounts commute — 20% then 10% gives exactly the same selling price as 10% then 20%, because you are multiplying the same two fractions. Use that freedom to apply whichever discount cancels against your marked price first, so you never carry an ugly intermediate number.

Compute the SURVIVING fraction, not the discount, all the way through: 25% and 20% off is ×3/4 × 4/5 = 3/5 surviving. Then convert once at the end: 3/5 surviving = 40% discount. One conversion instead of two, and the cancellation is usually visible by eye.

For 'equal successive discounts of x% twice', the single equivalent is 2x − x²/100: two 10%s give 19%, two 20%s give 36%, two 25%s give 43.75%. Knowing the first two by heart covers a lot of exam questions instantly.

Set MP = 100 for pure-discount questions and CP = 100 for profit questions. Choosing the right anchor is worth about 15 seconds — anchoring at CP in a three-discount question forces you to carry fractions you never needed.
When the numbers are awkward, anchor at the LCM instead of 100: for discounts of 12½% and 20%, take MP = 400 (divisible by 8 and 5) and every intermediate stays a whole number.
traps: Adding successive discounts. 20% and 10% is 28%, not 30%. Three discounts of 25%, 20% and 10% is 46%, not 55%. The additive answer is deliberately placed in the option list every single time.

Applying the discount to cost price. Discount is defined as MP − SP and has no relationship to CP. If a question ever says 'discount on cost price', re-read it — you have almost certainly read a markup as a discount.
Assuming a 20% markup is cancelled by a 20% discount. Marking up 20% and discounting 20% gives 100 → 120 → 96, a 4% LOSS, because the two percentages act on different bases.
Reporting the surviving percentage as the answer to 'find the equivalent single discount'. In worked example A the surviving fraction is 60% and the discount is 40%; both numbers will be options.
Missing that a 'cash discount' or 'additional discount for immediate payment' is a THIRD multiplier applied to the already-reduced price, not an addition to the earlier discounts (worked example F).
Reading 'the shopkeeper marks his goods at 40% above the selling price' as 'above the cost price'. The base word after 'above' decides the entire chain — circle it before you write anything.

q-si.whatItIs: Interest computed only on the original principal, never on interest already earned. SI = P × R × T / 100, and Amount A = P + SI = P(1 + RT/100), where P is the principal in rupees, R the rate percent per annum and T the time in years. The one structural fact that makes this topic fast is that simple interest is LINEAR: the interest earned in year 1 is exactly the interest earned in year 7. Every non-trivial exam question exploits that linearity — sums that amount to different values after different periods, sums that become n times themselves, and sums split into two parts at two different rates. In IBPS Clerk it appears both as a standalone word problem and, more often in Mains, as the second half of a comparison question against compound interest.
q-si.coreMethod:
THE RT-AS-ONE-NUMBER METHOD — 4 steps:
1. Multiply rate by time FIRST and treat the product as a single total percentage. 8% for 5 years is simply 40% of the principal. 7.5% for 4 years is 30%. 12% for 2½ years is 30%. This removes one division by 100 and one multiplication from every problem.
2. Apply that total percentage to P using a fraction where possible (40% = 2/5, 30% = 3/10, 25% = 1/4).
3. Decide from the wording whether the question wants INTEREST or AMOUNT, and circle the word before computing.
4. If time is given in months or days, convert to a fraction of a year immediately (9 months = 3/4 year, 73 days = 1/5 year) and keep it as a fraction.

THE LINEARITY METHOD — for any question giving two amounts at two times:
Yearly interest = (A₂ − A₁) / (T₂ − T₁). Then P = A₁ − T₁ × (yearly interest), and R = (yearly interest / P) × 100. Three subtractions, no equations.

THE MULTIPLE-OF-PRINCIPAL METHOD — 'a sum becomes n times itself in T years':
The interest earned equals (n − 1) × P, so R × T / 100 = n − 1, giving R = (n − 1) × 100 / T and T = (n − 1) × 100 / R.

THE TWO-PART METHOD — a sum split between two rates:
Either set up one equation in x, or use alligation on the rates with the mean rate = total interest / total principal. Both are shown below.

WORKED EXAMPLES (all computed and checked):

A. Direct. P = Rs.12,000 at 7.5% per annum for 4 years.
RT = 30%. SI = 12,000 × 3/10 = Rs.3,600. Amount = Rs.15,600. ✓

B. Two amounts, two times. A sum amounts to Rs.7,440 in 3 years and Rs.8,400 in 5 years at simple interest. Find the principal and the rate.
Difference = 8,400 − 7,440 = 960 over 2 years → yearly interest = 480. P = 7,440 − 3 × 480 = 7,440 − 1,440 = Rs.6,000. R = 480/6,000 × 100 = 8% per annum. Check: 6,000 at 8% for 5 years gives 2,400 interest, amount 8,400. ✓

C. Multiple of principal. A sum becomes 3 times itself in 16 years at simple interest. Find the rate.
Interest = 2P, so R × 16/100 = 2 → R = 12.5% per annum. Check: 12.5% × 16 = 200% of P as interest, so the amount is 3P. ✓

D. Two parts at two rates. Rs.15,000 is split into two parts, one lent at 6% and the other at 10% simple interest. The total annual interest is Rs.1,240. Find each part.
Let x be the part at 6%: 0.06x + 0.10(15,000 − x) = 1,240 → 1,500 − 0.04x = 1,240 → x = 6,500. So Rs.6,500 at 6% and Rs.8,500 at 10%. Check: 390 + 850 = 1,240. ✓
Alligation check: mean rate = 1,240/15,000 = 8.267%. Ratio = (10 − 8.267) : (8.267 − 6) = 1.733 : 2.267 = 13 : 17. 15,000 × 13/30 = 6,500. ✓ Same answer.

E. Backwards. The simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 8% per annum is Rs.2,400. Find the sum.
RT = 24%, so 24% of P = 2,400 → P = Rs.10,000. ✓

F. Rate change. A sum of Rs.8,000 is lent at 5% for the first 2 years and 9% for the next 3 years. Total interest?
8,000 × 10% + 8,000 × 27% = 800 + 2,160 = Rs.2,960. Because SI never compounds, the two blocks simply add. ✓
tricks: Collapse R and T into one percentage before touching the principal. '9% for 2 years 8 months' becomes 9 × 8/3 = 24% of P — one multiplication instead of a three-term fraction. Across a full paper this is the single largest time saving in the topic.

R and T are interchangeable in simple interest: 4% for 6 years and 6% for 4 years give identical interest. When a question asks 'at what rate would the same interest be earned in 5 years instead of 8', you can swap rather than re-solve.

For 'becomes n times in T years', use R = (n − 1) × 100 / T directly. Doubling in 8 years is 12.5%; tripling in 16 years is 12.5% as well (worked example C). Two related questions collapse into one formula.

When two different multiples are given ('doubles in 8 years, in how many years does it become 5 times'), use (n₁ − 1)/T₁ = (n₂ − 1)/T₂. Here 1/8 = 4/T₂ → T₂ = 32 years. No principal and no rate needed at all.

In two-amounts-at-two-times problems, never set up simultaneous equations. Subtract the amounts, divide by the year gap, and you have the yearly interest — the principal then comes from one more subtraction (worked example B is a 25-second question this way).
For two-part lending, alligation on the RATES gives the split ratio directly; it is faster than the equation whenever the two rates are integers and the mean is easy.
traps: Treating a stated AMOUNT as the principal. 'A sum amounts to Rs.7,440 in 3 years' means principal plus interest equals 7,440. Plugging 7,440 in as P produces a number that is sitting in the option list.
Leaving time in months when the rate is per annum. 9 months is 3/4 of a year, not 9. This is the most common single arithmetic error in the topic and it inflates the answer twelve-fold.
Reading 'the sum doubles' as 'interest equals 2P'. Doubling means the AMOUNT is 2P, so the interest is only 1P. Tripling means interest = 2P. Always subtract one from the multiple.

Halving the rate and doubling the time because the question says interest is 'payable half-yearly'. That adjustment belongs to compound interest. Simple interest is unaffected by the payment frequency — the answer is identical.
In two-part problems, applying the total interest to only one part. In worked example D the Rs.1,240 is the combined annual interest on both Rs.6,500 and Rs.8,500.

Mixing SI and CI within one Mains comparison question — computing the first-year interest correctly (they are equal) and then carrying it forward as if the second year also matched. They diverge from year 2 onwards.

q-si.weightageNote: Interest (simple and compound together) is a standing member of the 10-12 arithmetic word problems in the 35-question Prelims Numerical Ability section, typically contributing 1-2 questions per paper, with a similar presence in the 40-question Mains Quantitative Aptitude paper. Simple interest is the cheaper half to master — most questions resolve in under 40 seconds once the RT-collapse is automatic — and it also supplies the principal in many CI-versus-SI comparison questions, so it earns its tier-1 place on cost-to-learn rather than on raw question count.

q-ci.whatItIs: Interest computed on the principal plus all interest accumulated so far, so the base grows each period. Amount A = P(1 + R/100)^n, and Compound Interest CI = A − P, where n is the number of compounding periods. At IBPS Clerk level the exponent is almost always 2 or 3, and the rates are chosen from the friendly family (5%, 8⅓%, 10%, 12½%, 20%, 25%) precisely so the arithmetic can be done by hand in under a minute. Beyond the plain calculation, three sub-forms recur: the difference between CI and SI on the same sum, half-yearly or quarterly compounding, and equal annual instalments. Compounding frequency is the exam's favourite lever: 'compounded half-yearly' halves the rate and doubles the number of periods.
q-ci.coreMethod:
THE FRACTION-MULTIPLIER METHOD — 4 steps (use this as the default):
1. Convert the rate to a growth fraction: 5% → ×21/20, 8⅓% → ×13/12, 10% → ×11/10, 12½% → ×9/8, 16⅔% → ×7/6, 20% → ×6/5, 25% → ×5/4.
2. Multiply the principal by that fraction once per period, cancelling as you go. IBPS chooses principals divisible by the denominator raised to the power n, so every intermediate is a whole number.
3. Subtract the principal at the end if the question asks for interest rather than amount.
4. Circle 'amount' or 'interest' in the question before you start — both appear in the five options.

THE TOTAL-PERCENTAGE METHOD — for 2-year questions, faster still:
Two years at R% is a total growth of (2R + R²/100)%. Memorise: 5% → 10.25%, 10% → 21%, 12½% → 26.5625%, 20% → 44%, 25% → 56.25%. One multiplication and you are done.
For three years, apply the two-year figure and then the rate once more using a + b + ab/100.

THE CI − SI DIFFERENCE FORMULAE:
For 2 years: difference = P × (R/100)².
For 3 years: difference = P × (R/100)² × (300 + R)/100.
These are different formulae — using the 2-year one on a 3-year question is the topic's commonest error.

COMPOUNDING FREQUENCY: half-yearly → rate becomes R/2 and periods become 2n. Quarterly → R/4 and 4n. Do this substitution FIRST, before any arithmetic.

WORKED EXAMPLES (all computed and checked):

A. Plain 2-year CI. P = Rs.8,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years.
8,000 × 11/10 × 11/10 = Rs.9,680, so CI = Rs.1,680. Total-percentage check: 21% of 8,000 = 1,680. ✓

B. Awkward-looking rate made easy. P = Rs.6,400 at 12½% per annum for 2 years.
6,400 × 9/8 × 9/8 = 6,400 × 81/64 = Rs.8,100. CI = Rs.1,700. ✓ (Note how the fraction turns a hostile rate into two clean divisions.)

C. CI − SI, two years. The difference between CI and SI on a sum for 2 years at 8% per annum is Rs.128. Find the sum.
P × (8/100)² = 128 → P × 64/10,000 = 128 → P = Rs.20,000. Check: SI = 20,000 × 16% = 3,200; CI = 20,000 × 1.08² − 20,000 = 23,328 − 20,000 = 3,328; difference = 128. ✓

D. Consecutive amounts → find rate and principal. A sum amounts to Rs.9,680 in 2 years and Rs.10,648 in 3 years at compound interest. Find the rate and the sum.
The third-year interest is 10,648 − 9,680 = 968, earned on 9,680, so R = 968/9,680 × 100 = 10%. Then P = 9,680 ÷ (11/10)² = 9,680 × 100/121 = Rs.8,000. ✓ (Consistent with example A.)

E. Half-yearly. Rs.12,000 at 10% per annum compounded half-yearly for 1 year.
Rate becomes 5% per half-year, periods become 2. A = 12,000 × 21/20 × 21/20 = Rs.13,230. CI = Rs.1,230. Note that annual compounding would have given only Rs.1,200. ✓

F. CI − SI, three years. P = Rs.5,000 at 10% per annum for 3 years.
CI: 5,000 × 1.331 = 6,655 → CI = 1,655. SI = 5,000 × 30% = 1,500. Difference = Rs.155. Formula check: 5,000 × (10/100)² × 310/100 = 5,000 × 0.01 × 3.1 = 155. ✓

G. Changing rate. Rs.10,000 at 10% in the first year and 12% in the second.
10,000 × 11/10 × 28/25 = 11,000 × 28/25 = Rs.12,320. CI = Rs.2,320. This is NOT the same as 11% for two years, which would give 12,321. ✓
tricks: Learn the two-year growth percentages by heart (10% → 21%, 20% → 44%, 25% → 56.25%, 5% → 10.25%). A two-year CI question then becomes a single multiplication and lands in about 20 seconds instead of 50.

The fastest CI − SI check for 2 years: the difference equals the FIRST YEAR'S interest multiplied by R%. At 10% on Rs.8,000 the first-year interest is 800, so the difference is 80 — and indeed CI 1,680 minus SI 1,600 equals 80. It matches P(R/100)² exactly and is easier to do mentally.

Two consecutive amounts hand you the rate for free: R% = (Aₙ₊₁ − Aₙ) / Aₙ × 100, because the gap between consecutive amounts is one year's interest on the earlier amount. Worked example D is a 20-second question using this.

Choose fraction multipliers over decimals whenever the rate is 8⅓%, 12½%, 16⅔% or 6¼%. Multiplying by 9/8 twice is trivial; multiplying by 1.125 twice by hand is not, and the decimal route is where careless errors enter.
For half-yearly and quarterly, write the substituted rate and period on your rough sheet BEFORE any calculation — 'R = 5, n = 2' — so you cannot half-apply the adjustment.

When the principal is not divisible by the denominator, scale: for 12½% take P in multiples of 64 for 2 years and 512 for 3 years. If the given principal is not, work with the growth percentage instead of the fraction.
traps: Applying the 2-year CI − SI formula P(R/100)² to a 3-year question. The 3-year formula carries an extra factor of (300 + R)/100 — at 10% that is 3.1 times larger, as worked examples C and F show side by side.

Half-yearly compounding: halving the rate but forgetting to double the number of periods, or doubling the periods while leaving the rate at the annual figure. Either half of the adjustment alone gives a wrong answer that appears in the options.
Averaging two different annual rates. 10% then 12% is not 11% for two years — worked example G gives Rs.12,320 against Rs.12,321. The gap is small by design, so the wrong answer looks defensible.
'Compound interest for the third year' means A₃ − A₂ only, not the total CI over three years. In worked example D the third-year interest is Rs.968 while the three-year CI is Rs.2,648.

Reporting the AMOUNT when the question asks for the INTEREST. In worked example A both 9,680 and 1,680 will be options, and under a 20-minute sectional clock this misread is more common than any arithmetic slip.

Assuming SI and CI are equal for the first year and therefore treating a one-year CI question as needing the compound formula. For n = 1 they genuinely are equal — but only for n = 1, and only when compounding is annual. If it is half-yearly, one year of CI already exceeds one year of SI (worked example E: Rs.1,230 against Rs.1,200).
q-ci.timeTarget: 30-40 seconds for a plain 2-year CI using the memorised growth percentage. 45-55 seconds for CI − SI, consecutive-amount and 3-year questions. 60-70 seconds for half-yearly, changing-rate or instalment questions. Anything past 80 seconds should be abandoned — CI questions rarely have a partial-credit path and a guess costs 0.25.
q-ci.masteryCheck: 15 questions in 11 minutes with 13 or more correct, including at least two half-yearly and two CI − SI questions. Separately, without writing anything: state the 2-year CI on Rs.6,000 at 20% (44% of 6,000 = Rs.2,640) and the CI − SI difference on Rs.4,500 at 10% for 2 years (first-year interest 450, times 10% = Rs.45). If either takes more than 15 seconds, the growth-percentage table is not yet memorised and every CI question in the paper will run 25 seconds long.
questionPatterns: P, R and n given (n = 2 or 3); find the compound interest or the amount. Five options containing both the amount and the interest.
The difference between compound and simple interest on a sum for 2 years (sometimes 3) at a given rate is stated; find the sum. Occasionally reversed — sum and rate given, find the difference.
A sum amounts to Rs.A₁ after n years and Rs.A₂ after n+1 years at compound interest; find the rate, or the original sum, or the amount after one further year.
Compounded half-yearly or quarterly for 1 or 1½ years at a given annual rate; find the amount, or find how much more it is than annual compounding would give.
Different rates in successive years (say 10%, 12% and 15%); find the final amount or the total interest.

Mains set/instalment form: a loan repaid in two or three equal annual instalments at a given rate — find the instalment or the sum borrowed; or a paragraph in which an SI figure fixes the principal that is then used for a CI sub-question.

q-ci.aiPrompt:
Act as a question setter for IBPS Clerk Prelims and Mains 2026, Numerical Ability. Generate 15 compound-interest questions.

STRICT FORMAT RULES:
- Every question must have EXACTLY FIVE options labelled (1) to (5). Exactly one is correct.
- Distribute as: 4 plain CI (n = 2 or 3, find CI or amount), 3 on the difference between CI and SI (two of them for 2 years, one for 3 years), 2 giving consecutive-year amounts and asking for the rate or the principal, 3 with half-yearly or quarterly compounding, 2 with the rate changing between years, 1 equal-annual-instalment question.
- Restrict rates to 5%, 8 1/3%, 10%, 12 1/2%, 20% or 25% so the arithmetic is hand-doable.
- Choose principals divisible by the relevant power of the growth-fraction denominator (e.g. multiples of 64 for 12 1/2% over 2 years) so every intermediate value is a whole number.
- Where the question asks for interest, put the corresponding AMOUNT among the wrong options, and vice versa.

SOLUTION RULES:
- SOLVE EVERY QUESTION YOURSELF FIRST and print the full working. The correct value must be one of the five printed options — verify numerically for all 15.
- Solve using fraction growth-multipliers (10% = x11/10, 12.5% = x9/8 and so on), showing the cancellation. Do not use decimal powers.
- For every half-yearly or quarterly question, state the substituted rate and the substituted number of periods on a separate line before computing.
- For the CI-minus-SI questions, use P(R/100)^2 for two years and P(R/100)^2 x (300+R)/100 for three years, and say explicitly which formula applies and why.
- All answers must be exact rupee amounts or terminate within two decimal places. Discard and regenerate any question with a recurring decimal.
q-ci.blockPlan: One and a half 4-hour days, scheduled immediately after simple interest. DAY 1 — Block 1 (60 min): derive A = P(1+R/100)^n, build the growth-fraction table and the two-year growth-percentage table, and drill both until recall is instant. Then 15 plain 2-year questions. Block 2 (60 min): 3-year questions and the consecutive-amount family, 20 questions, using the one-subtraction-one-division route for the rate. Block 3 (60 min): derive both CI − SI difference formulae yourself and verify each on a numerical example before use; then 20 difference questions, deliberately mixing 2-year and 3-year so you have to identify which formula applies. Block 4 (60 min): half-yearly and quarterly, 15 questions, writing the substituted rate and periods every time. HALF DAY 2 — Block 1 (60 min): changing rates and equal annual instalments, 15 questions. Block 2 (60 min): a 20-question timed mixed set at 50 seconds each, then a 10-question SI-versus-CI comparison set to make sure you never conflate the two. Refresh weekly with 8-10 questions; CI decays faster than SI because of the tables.

q-timework.whatItIs: How long a job takes when people of different speeds work on it, together or in sequence. One person who finishes a job in d days does 1/d of it per day — but you should almost never write that fraction. The exam-speed approach assigns the whole job a convenient number of UNITS (the LCM of the given days), which turns every rate into a whole number and every combination into simple addition. The topic covers: combined work, one person leaving or joining partway, efficiency comparisons ('twice as fast', '50% more efficient'), alternate-day working, the men-days scaling relation M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂, and wage distribution. Pipes and cistern (q-pipes) is the same engine with negative rates, so mastering this topic makes that one nearly free.
q-timework.coreMethod:
THE LCM-UNITS METHOD — 4 steps, use it for every single question:
1. TOTAL WORK = LCM of all the day-figures given in the question. If A takes 12 days and B takes 18, total work = 36 units.
2. EFFICIENCY of each worker = total work ÷ their days. A = 36/12 = 3 units/day, B = 36/18 = 2 units/day.
3. COMBINE by adding efficiencies for everyone working simultaneously. A + B = 5 units/day. Subtract for anyone undoing work.
4. TIME = work remaining ÷ combined efficiency. 36/5 = 7.2 days.
No fractions appear anywhere. This is the whole topic.

TWO SUPPORTING RELATIONS:
• Efficiency is INVERSELY proportional to time. If A is twice as efficient as B, A's efficiency : B's = 2 : 1, so A's time : B's time = 1 : 2. '50% more efficient' means efficiency ratio 3 : 2 and time ratio 2 : 3.
• Man-days scaling: M₁ × D₁ × H₁ / W₁ = M₂ × D₂ × H₂ / W₂. Use it whenever the number of workers changes and no individual rate is given.

WAGES: split in the ratio of WORK ACTUALLY DONE, which is efficiency × number of days each person worked. Never in the ratio of days taken.

WORKED EXAMPLES (all computed and checked):

A. Basic combination. A does a job in 12 days, B in 18 days. Together?
LCM = 36. A = 3, B = 2, together = 5/day. Time = 36/5 = 7.2 days = 7⅕ days. ✓

B. Backing out one worker. A and B together finish in 8 days; A alone takes 12 days. B alone?
LCM = 24. Together = 3/day, A = 2/day, so B = 1/day → B alone takes 24 days. ✓

C. Efficiency ratio. A is twice as efficient as B and together they finish in 14 days. A alone?
A : B = 2 : 1, so combined = 3 units/day. Total work = 3 × 14 = 42 units. A alone = 42/2 = 21 days. Check: B alone = 42 days; 1/21 + 1/42 = 3/42 = 1/14. ✓

D. Someone leaves. A, B and C can do a job in 10, 12 and 15 days. All three start together but A leaves after 2 days. How long does the whole job take?
LCM = 60. A = 6, B = 5, C = 4. First 2 days at 15/day = 30 units done. Remaining 30 units at 9/day (B + C) = 30/9 = 3⅓ days. Total = 5⅓ days. ✓

E. Man-days scaling. 12 men complete a job in 18 days. After 6 days, 4 more men join. How many MORE days to finish?
Total = 12 × 18 = 216 man-days. Done in 6 days = 72 man-days. Remaining = 144 man-days with 16 men = 9 days. ✓

F. Alternate days. A can do a job in 9 days and B in 18 days. They work on alternate days starting with A. Total time?
LCM = 18. A = 2/day, B = 1/day. Each 2-day block = 3 units. Five blocks (10 days) = 15 units. Day 11 is A's: 15 + 2 = 17. Day 12 is B's: 17 + 1 = 18 units — complete. Total = 12 days. ✓

G. Wages. A alone can do a job in 6 days, B alone in 8 days. With C's help all three finish in 3 days. The total wage is Rs.3,200. What is C's share?
LCM = 24. A = 4, B = 3, all three = 24/3 = 8/day. So C = 8 − 4 − 3 = 1/day. Wage ratio A : B : C = 4 : 3 : 1. C's share = 3,200 × 1/8 = Rs.400. ✓
tricks: Never write 1/12 + 1/18. Setting total work to the LCM removes every fraction from the page and turns a 60-second question into a 30-second one; the arithmetic error rate collapses along with the time.

For alternate-day problems, compute the 2-day block first, divide the total by the block, then finish the tail one day at a time. Crucially, check whether the job completes MID-DAY: if 2 units remain and the worker on duty does 3 per day, the answer carries a half-day (e.g. 11.5 days), and that fraction will be one of the five options.

Efficiency ratio inverts to time ratio, so 'A is thrice as efficient as B' means B takes three times as long. Set the combined efficiency as the sum of the ratio parts and multiply by the given joint time to get total work in one step — worked example C never needs individual days.

Man-days is a conserved quantity when no individual rates are given: total man-days done plus total man-days remaining equals the original product. Worked example E takes two subtractions and one division, with no LCM needed at all.

Wages follow work done, so once you have the efficiency figures the wage ratio is already on your page — no extra computation. In worked example G, finding C's efficiency (1 unit) and the total (8 units) is the entire question.

When a question says 'A leaves 3 days BEFORE the work is completed', let T be the total time: A works for T − 3 days and the others for T. Set up units-done = total and solve for T. This differs structurally from 'A leaves after 3 days' and needs the variable.
traps: Splitting wages in the ratio of DAYS TAKEN instead of work done. If A takes 6 days and B takes 8, the wage ratio is 4 : 3 (their efficiencies), not 6 : 8. The inverted answer is always among the options.
Confusing 'A is twice as efficient as B' with 'A takes twice as long as B'. These are opposite statements and produce reciprocal answers.
Adding times instead of efficiencies. A at 12 days and B at 18 days together take 7.2 days, not 30 and not 15. Only rates add.

In alternate-day problems, ignoring who starts. Nine days for A and eighteen for B starting with A gives 12 days (worked example F); starting with B the first 10 days give 15 units, day 11 (A) gives 17, day 12 (B) gives 18 — also 12 days here, but with unequal efficiencies and a different total the two orders often differ by a day, so always re-check the tail rather than assuming symmetry.

'A leaves after 3 days' versus 'A leaves 3 days before completion' — the first is a fixed 3 days of A's work, the second is an unknown that must be solved for. Reading one as the other changes the answer entirely.
In man-days questions, adding the extra workers from day one instead of from the day they joined. In worked example E the 16 men work only the final stretch; the first 6 days are at 12 men.
q-timework.timeTarget: 35-45 seconds for basic combination, backing-out and efficiency-ratio questions. 55-70 seconds for leaves-partway, alternate-day and wage questions. In Prelims, where 35 questions share 20 minutes, treat anything past 75 seconds as a skip — this topic has many one-line questions and it is better to bank two of those than to force one hard one.
q-timework.masteryCheck: 15 questions in 12 minutes with 13 or more correct, all solved in LCM units with no fraction written anywhere on the rough sheet. questionPatterns: Two or three individual times given; find the time taken working together, or find one person's time given the joint time and the others'.
Efficiency comparison: 'A is x times as efficient as B' or 'A is p% more efficient than B', plus a joint completion time; find an individual time.
One or more workers join or leave partway: 'all start together, A leaves after n days' or 'A leaves n days before completion' — find the total time or the remaining time.
Men-days scaling: 'x men complete a job in d days; how many men are needed to finish it in d' days', often with hours per day added as a third factor.
Alternate-day or rotating working, with the starting worker specified; find the total number of days, with fractional-day answers among the options.

Wage distribution: a total payment split among two or three workers, with one worker's contribution given only implicitly through the joint time; find one person's share. Also appears in Mains as a paragraph set combining a completion-time question and a wage question on the same data.

q-pipes.whatItIs: Time and work wearing a different costume. A pipe that fills a tank in t hours works at 1/t of the tank per hour; a pipe that empties it works at −1/t. Every question is a matter of adding positive and negative rates and dividing the capacity by the net rate. The recurring sub-forms are: several pipes open together, a leak that slows a filling pipe, a pipe closed partway through, pipes opened alternately for one minute each, capacity questions where an inlet is quoted in litres per minute, and tanks that start partly filled. Because the machinery is identical to q-timework, this topic is cheap to add once that one is done — the only genuinely new content is sign discipline.
q-pipes.coreMethod:
THE SIGNED-LCM METHOD — 5 steps:
1. CAPACITY = LCM of all the given fill and empty times. Write it in a box at the top.
2. RATE of each pipe = capacity ÷ its time. Write inlet rates as POSITIVE and outlet or leak rates as NEGATIVE, in a single column so the signs are visible.
3. NET RATE = the algebraic sum of the pipes that are actually open during the period you are considering.
4. CHECK THE SIGN of the net rate before dividing. Positive means the tank fills; negative means it empties and a question asking 'time to fill' has no positive answer — the option list will contain 'cannot be filled' or 'never'.
5. TIME = (work remaining) ÷ (net rate). 'Work remaining' is the full capacity only if the tank starts empty — read for words like 'half full' or 'one-third filled'.

THE LEAK SHORTCUT: if a pipe alone fills in t₁ hours but takes t₂ hours because of a leak, the leak alone empties a full tank in t₁t₂/(t₂ − t₁) hours.

UNITS DISCIPLINE: when one rate is in litres per minute and another is per hour, convert to a single time unit BEFORE writing the equation. This is where litre-capacity questions are won or lost.

WORKED EXAMPLES (all computed and checked):

A. Three pipes, one outlet. Pipe A fills a tank in 12 hours, B fills it in 15 hours and C empties it in 20 hours. All three are opened together. How long to fill?
LCM = 60. A = +5, B = +4, C = −3. Net = +6 per hour. Time = 60/6 = 10 hours. ✓

B. The leak family. A pipe can fill a tank in 6 hours, but because of a leak it takes 8 hours. How long would the leak alone take to empty a full tank?
LCM = 24. Pipe = +4, pipe-with-leak = +3, so leak = −1 per hour → 24 hours. Shortcut check: 6 × 8 / (8 − 6) = 48/2 = 24 hours. ✓

C. A pipe closed partway. Two pipes fill a tank in 20 minutes and 30 minutes respectively. Both are opened together, but the first is closed after some time and the tank is full in 18 minutes altogether. After how many minutes was the first pipe closed?
LCM = 60. A = +3, B = +2. B runs the whole 18 minutes: 2 × 18 = 36 units. The remaining 60 − 36 = 24 units came from A at 3/minute → A ran for 8 minutes. Answer: closed after 8 minutes. ✓

D. Litres per minute. A tank has a leak that would empty it in 12 hours. An inlet admitting 6 litres per minute is opened, and now the tank empties in 20 hours. Find the capacity.
Inlet = 6 litres/min = 360 litres/hour. Leak rate = C/12 per hour. Net emptying rate = C/20 per hour.
C/12 − 360 = C/20 → C(1/12 − 1/20) = 360 → C(5 − 3)/60 = 360 → C/30 = 360 → C = 10,800 litres. ✓ Check: leak drains 900 l/h, inlet adds 360 l/h, net 540 l/h, and 10,800/540 = 20 hours. ✓

E. Alternate minutes. Pipe A fills a tank in 10 minutes and pipe B in 15 minutes. They are opened alternately for one minute each, starting with A. How long to fill?
LCM = 30. A = +3, B = +2. Each 2-minute block adds 5 units. Five blocks (10 minutes) = 25 units. Minute 11 is A's: 25 + 3 = 28. Minute 12 is B's: B adds 2, reaching exactly 30. Total = 12 minutes. ✓

F. Partly-filled tank. A tank is one-third full. Pipe A fills it in 18 minutes and pipe B empties it in 9 minutes. If both are opened, will the tank fill or empty, and in how long?
LCM = 18. A = +1, B = −2. Net = −1 per minute. The tank currently holds 6 units, so it EMPTIES in 6 minutes. A question asking 'time to fill' here would be answered 'the tank can never be filled'. ✓
tricks: Write every rate in one vertical column with its sign attached, inlets above outlets. Sign errors are the only real difficulty in this topic, and a two-column layout eliminates them at the cost of about three seconds.

Use the leak shortcut t₁t₂/(t₂ − t₁) for the whole 'pipe alone versus pipe with leak' family — a 6-and-8-hour question becomes 48/2 = 24 in about ten seconds, against roughly forty seconds for the full LCM route.

For 'one pipe closed partway, tank full in T minutes', compute the always-open pipe's total contribution over the full T first, subtract from capacity, and divide the balance by the closed pipe's rate. That gives the running time directly, as in worked example C, with no equation.
Check the sign of the net rate before doing any division. If it is negative or zero, you already know the answer is 'cannot be filled' and you have saved the whole calculation.

In litres-per-minute questions, convert the inlet to litres per HOUR immediately if the leak is quoted in hours (6 l/min → 360 l/h). Doing this before writing the equation prevents the single commonest error in the capacity family.

For alternate-minute problems, compute the 2-minute block, then handle the tail minute by minute — and allow for a partial minute. If 2 units remain and the pipe on duty delivers 3 per minute, the answer is a further 2/3 of a minute, and such fractional answers do appear in the option list.
traps: Adding an outlet pipe's rate instead of subtracting it. In worked example A, treating C as an inlet gives 60/12 = 5 hours instead of 10 — and 5 hours will be one of the five options.

Assuming a tank always fills. When the outlets outrun the inlets the net rate is negative and the correct answer is that the tank cannot be filled, or that it empties. Worked example F is exactly this case.

Applying the full LCM capacity to a tank that is already partly filled. 'The tank is one-third full' means only two-thirds remains to be filled — or, if it is emptying, only one-third remains to be drained.
Mixing minutes and hours in the same rate column. A leak quoted in hours and an inlet quoted in litres per minute must be brought to a common unit before they can be combined (worked example D).

Reading 'pipe A can empty a FULL tank in 20 minutes' and applying that 20 minutes to a tank that is only half full. The stated time always refers to the full capacity; scale it to whatever is actually in the tank.
In the closed-partway family, answering with the total time (18 minutes) rather than the time the pipe ran (8 minutes), or vice versa. Circle which one the question asks for before computing.

q-tsd.whatItIs: Every question in this family is one equation: Speed = Distance / Time. What makes it an exam topic is not the formula but the three shapes IBPS wraps around it: (a) same distance covered at two different speeds, giving a late/early time gap; (b) average speed over a journey split into parts; (c) two bodies moving toward or away from each other, where you work with relative speed. It is also the parent topic of Boats & Streams and Trains — the same three shapes reappear there with a stream or a train length added. In Clerk Prelims it shows up as a plain 2-3 line word problem; in Mains it is often bundled into an arithmetic set or a caselet with one TSD sub-question.
q-tsd.coreMethod:
1. WRITE THE UNIT FIRST. If the answer is asked in metres/seconds, convert every km/h to m/s at the very start using x5/18. If everything is in km and hours, do not convert at all. Memorise: 18 km/h = 5 m/s, 36 = 10, 54 = 15, 72 = 20, 90 = 25, 108 = 30.
2. IDENTIFY WHICH QUANTITY IS CONSTANT. In almost every question one of D, S, T is fixed. Same distance is the most common. Say it out loud: 'distance is the same'.
3. IF DISTANCE IS CONSTANT, USE INVERSE RATIO, NOT ALGEBRA. Speeds in ratio a:b means times in ratio b:a. Do not set up D/a - D/b = t; set up the ratio and match one part to the given time gap.
   Worked: walking at 5 km/h a student is 6 minutes LATE; at 6 km/h he is 4 minutes EARLY. Speeds 5:6, so times 6:5. Difference = 1 part. Actual time gap = 6 + 4 = 10 minutes, so 1 part = 10 min. Time at 5 km/h = 6 parts = 60 min = 1 hour. Distance = 5 x 1 = 5 km. (Check: 5/6 h = 50 min, which is 4 min less than the 54-min schedule. Correct.)
4. IF THE QUESTION GIVES A PERCENTAGE CHANGE IN SPEED, FLIP THE FRACTION. Speed becomes 5/4 of original (a 25% rise) means time becomes 4/5 of original (a 20% fall). Speed becomes 3/4 (25% drop) means time becomes 4/3 (a 33 1/3% rise). Never compute the distance for these.
5. AVERAGE SPEED = TOTAL DISTANCE / TOTAL TIME. Always. For two EQUAL distances at speeds a and b, the shortcut is 2ab/(a+b). For three equal parts at a, b, c it is 3abc/(ab+bc+ca).
   Worked: 60 km/h out, 40 km/h back. Average = 2(60)(40)/100 = 48 km/h.
6. IF THE TIMES ARE EQUAL INSTEAD OF THE DISTANCES, the average IS the plain average (a+b)/2. Check which one the question gave before choosing.
7. FOR TWO BODIES: moving toward each other or crossing, add the speeds; moving in the same direction (chasing), subtract. Time to meet = gap / relative speed.
8. FOR THE 'AFTER MEETING' PATTERN: two people start from opposite ends at the same time; after meeting, A needs t1 more hours and B needs t2 more hours. Then Speed A : Speed B = root(t2) : root(t1).
   Worked: after meeting A takes 4 h, B takes 9 h. Ratio = root9 : root4 = 3:2. (Verify: meeting happened at 4 x 3/2 = 6 hours.)
9. STOPPAGE QUESTIONS: if a bus runs at x km/h without stops and y km/h with stops, stoppage time per hour = (x - y)/x hours. Example: 60 and 45 gives 15/60 h = 15 minutes per hour.
tricks: Inverse-ratio in one line: for the late/early pattern, speeds a:b give times b:a, and the difference of the two time-parts equals the TOTAL of the late and early minutes. One subtraction, one division, done in about 20 seconds. Setting up D/a - D/b wastes 30-40 seconds and invites an LCM slip.

Convert once, at the start, never mid-solution. Deciding 'this is a metres-and-seconds question' before writing anything eliminates the single most common wrong answer, which is the right number in the wrong unit.

Percentage-change questions need no distance at all: speed x k means time x 1/k. 20% faster = 5/6 the time (a 16 2/3% saving); 20% slower = 5/4 the time (a 25% increase). Reading the answer straight off the reciprocal saves the whole equation.

When the five options are far apart, estimate: 2ab/(a+b) always lies strictly between a and b and always closer to the SMALLER speed. If only one option sits between the two speeds and below their plain average, that is the answer and you have spent 10 seconds.
Keep distances in the numerator as fractions, not decimals. 40/3 km/h beaten into 13.33 costs time and rounding error; carry the fraction to the last step, where it usually cancels.
traps: Adding the late and early gaps wrongly. 'Six minutes late' and 'four minutes early' is a gap of TEN minutes, not two. Aspirants who subtract get 1 km instead of 5 km in the worked example above, and 1 km is almost always one of the five options.
Treating (a+b)/2 as average speed when the two DISTANCES are equal. For 60 and 40 the answer is 48, not 50, and 50 will be one of the options specifically to catch this.

Multiplying by 18/5 when you needed 5/18. km/h to m/s is x5/18 (the number gets SMALLER); m/s to km/h is x18/5 (the number gets BIGGER). If your converted speed went up when going from km/h to m/s, you flipped it.

Leaving minutes in an equation whose other terms are in hours. '12 minutes' inside a km/h equation must be 1/5, not 12. This produces answers off by a factor of 60, which look absurd but still get circled under clock pressure.

Assuming a body that 'starts 2 hours later' covers the same time. In catch-up questions the head start is a DISTANCE (early speed x head-start hours), and that distance is what the relative speed has to eat up. Forgetting to convert the head start from hours into km is the standard error.
Applying root(t2):root(t1) when the two people did NOT start at the same moment. That result is derived assuming simultaneous start; if starts are staggered, go back to the basic equation.

Average speed: 30-40 seconds. Two-body relative speed or 'after meeting': 60-75 seconds. In Prelims, if a TSD question crosses 75 seconds, leave it and move on — the 20-minute sectional clock does not forgive one stubborn question.

Second check: state instantly that a 20% increase in speed cuts time by 16 2/3%, and that the average speed for equal distances at 30 and 20 km/h is 24 km/h, not 25. questionPatterns: Late/early: 'Walking at 3/4 of his usual speed, a man reaches office 20 minutes late. Find his usual time.' (Speed 3/4 -> time 4/3 -> extra 1/3 of usual time = 20 min -> usual time = 60 min.)
Average speed with equal halves: 'A car covers the first half of a 300 km journey at 50 km/h and the second half at 75 km/h. Find the average speed.' (2 x 50 x 75/125 = 60 km/h.)

Two-part journey with total time: 'A man covers 480 km partly at 40 km/h and partly at 60 km/h, taking 10 hours in all. Find the distance covered at 40 km/h.' (40t + 60(10-t) = 480 -> t = 6 h -> 240 km.)

Head start / catch-up: 'A starts at 8 a.m. at 30 km/h; B follows the same route at 10 a.m. at 45 km/h. At what time does B overtake A?' (Head start = 60 km; relative speed 15 km/h; 4 hours after 10 a.m. = 2 p.m.)
Stoppage: 'Excluding stoppages a bus averages 54 km/h; including stoppages, 45 km/h. How many minutes per hour does it stop?' ((54-45)/54 h = 10 minutes.)

After-meeting ratio: 'Two trains start simultaneously from A and B towards each other; after meeting they reach B and A in 9 and 16 hours respectively. Find the ratio of their speeds.' (root16 : root9 = 4:3.)

q-boats.whatItIs: Time, Speed & Distance with one extra term. A boat has a speed in still water (call it u) and the river has a current speed (v). Going with the current — downstream — the boat's effective speed is u+v. Going against it — upstream — it is u-v. Every question is built by hiding one or two of u, v, downstream speed or upstream speed and giving you distances and times instead. The topic is small, closed and highly formulaic, which makes it one of the fastest scoring topics in the arithmetic block once the four relations are automatic. IBPS asks it as a standalone word problem, occasionally as one arm of a two-statement quantity-comparison question in Mains.
q-boats.coreMethod:
1. DEFINE FOUR SYMBOLS ON PAPER BEFORE READING THE NUMBERS: u = still-water speed, v = stream speed, D = u+v (downstream), U = u-v (upstream).
2. THE TWO REVERSE FORMULAS ARE THE WHOLE TOPIC: u = (D+U)/2 and v = (D-U)/2. Still-water speed is the AVERAGE of the two effective speeds; stream speed is HALF THE DIFFERENCE.
   Worked: a boat covers 24 km downstream in 2 hours and returns in 3 hours. D = 24/2 = 12, U = 24/3 = 8. So u = (12+8)/2 = 10 km/h and v = (12-8)/2 = 2 km/h.
3. IF THE SAME DISTANCE TAKES t_down AND t_up: u/v = (t_up + t_down)/(t_up - t_down). Use this when the question gives times but not the distance. Check with the numbers above: (3+2)/(3-2) = 5, and indeed 10/2 = 5.
4. IF THE QUESTION SAYS 'x km downstream in the same time as y km upstream', then D:U = x:y immediately, with no equation. From D:U you get u:v = (x+y):(x-y).
   Worked: he rows 4 km with the stream in the time he rows 3 km against it, and covers 48 km each way in 14 hours total. D:U = 4:3, so let D = 4k, U = 3k. 48/4k + 48/3k = 14 -> 12/k + 16/k = 14 -> 28/k = 14 -> k = 2. So D = 8, U = 6, u = 7 km/h, v = 1 km/h.
5. FOR THE 'TAKES t HOURS MORE UPSTREAM' PATTERN, use d/(u-v) - d/(u+v) = t, which simplifies to 2dv/(u^2 - v^2) = t. Plug in and solve the quadratic in whichever variable is unknown.
   Worked: a boat takes 2 hours more to go 48 km upstream than to return downstream; stream = 2 km/h. 2(48)(2)/(u^2 - 4) = 2 -> 192 = 2u^2 - 8 -> u^2 = 100 -> u = 10 km/h. (Check: up = 8 -> 6 h; down = 12 -> 4 h; difference 2 h.)
6. ROUND-TRIP AVERAGE SPEED IS NOT u. Over a there-and-back trip of distance d each way, average speed = (u^2 - v^2)/u. With u = 10, v = 2 this is 96/10 = 9.6 km/h, not 10.
7. STILL WATER MEANS v = 0. A lake or pond question is pure TSD; do not invent a current.
8. IF THE OBJECT IS A SWIMMER, A SHIP, OR A MAN ROWING, nothing changes — the words differ, the algebra does not.
tricks: Read the sentence and immediately label each given speed as u, D or U. 'A boat travels at 12 km/h downstream' is D = 12, not u = 12. Doing this labelling before touching the arithmetic removes the single largest source of wrong answers in this topic and costs three seconds.

When both times for the same distance are given, go straight to u/v = (t_up + t_down)/(t_up - t_down) and skip computing D and U at all. On a question asking only for the RATIO, this is a single fraction and lands in about 15 seconds.

Halve-the-difference is faster than solving simultaneous equations. Given D and U, v = (D-U)/2 in one subtraction. Aspirants who write u + v = 12 and u - v = 8 and then eliminate are doing three lines of work for a one-line answer.

Use the 'same time' phrasing as a free ratio. 'Rows 4 km downstream in the time he rows 3 km upstream' hands you D:U = 4:3 with zero computation, because equal time means distance is directly proportional to speed.

For the 't hours more' pattern, note that 2dv/(u^2 - v^2) = t always produces u^2 as a clean number in IBPS papers. If your u^2 is not a perfect square, you have almost certainly mislabelled which speed is the stream — recheck rather than reaching for a calculator-style estimate.
traps: Treating the given 'speed of the boat' as still-water speed when the sentence actually described a downstream or upstream run. If the question says 'a boat covers 36 km in 3 hours going downstream', that 12 km/h is D; the still-water speed is smaller.
Computing v as (D-U) instead of (D-U)/2. In the 24 km example this gives 4 km/h instead of 2 km/h, and 4 will be among the five options.

Reporting the round-trip average speed as u. For a boat with u = 10 and v = 2 the round-trip average is 9.6 km/h; the current does not cancel out, because the slow leg takes longer and therefore carries more weight.
Mixing up which leg is longer in time. Upstream is the SLOWER leg, so it always takes MORE time. If your working has the upstream leg finishing faster, a sign is flipped.

Adding the stream speed twice — for example writing downstream speed as u + v and then, later in the same solution, adding v again to get the 'effective' speed. This shows up when a question involves a boat plus a floating object.
Forgetting that a floating object (a log, a bottle, a raft) has speed exactly v, not u+v. It has no engine; it moves at the stream's speed only.
